title: Beekeeping
materialsRequired: Hive (Langstroth or top-bar)
Smoker
Hive tool
Bee suit, gloves, veil
Sugar syrup (1:1 for spring, 2:1 for fall)
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Bees pollinate ⅓ of crops and produce honey, wax, and propolis. A single
hive can yield 20–40 kg of honey per year.

## Prerequisites

- [Simple Tools](../survival/simple-tools.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Hive (Langstroth or top-bar)
- Smoker
- Hive tool
- Bee suit, gloves, veil
- Sugar syrup (1:1 for spring, 2:1 for fall)

## Procedure

### Catching a Swarm

1. Find a swarm on a branch in spring.
2. Shake into a box; cover quickly.
3. Transfer to a hive at dusk.

### Building a Colony

1. Install the swarm; leave alone 1 week.
2. Inspect weekly in spring/summer.
3. Feed sugar syrup until comb is drawn.

### Harvesting Honey

1. Wait until ⅔ of cells are capped.
2. Brush bees off frames; use a bee escape board.
3. Uncapp with a knife.
4. Extract with a centrifuge or crush-and-strain.
5. Leave 15 kg honey for the colony's winter.

### Winterizing

1. Reduce entrance.
2. Feed 2:1 syrup in fall.
3. Insulate; ensure ventilation to prevent condensation.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Bee stings can cause anaphylaxis. Have epinephrine if allergic.
- Smoke calms but does not sedate; work slowly.
- Africanized bees are aggressive — do not work them without experience.

title: Composting
materialsRequired: Browns: dry leaves, straw, cardboard
Greens: kitchen scraps, grass clippings, manure
Pitchfork
Water
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Compost converts waste into fertility. It requires four ingredients:
carbon ("browns"), nitrogen ("greens"), water, and air.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Browns: dry leaves, straw, cardboard
- Greens: kitchen scraps, grass clippings, manure
- Pitchfork
- Water

## Procedure

### Pile Construction

1. Build a 1 m³ pile.
2. Layer 3 parts browns to 1 part greens.
3. Add water until the pile feels like a wrung-out sponge.
4. Turn every 3 days for hot compost (reaches 55–65°C).
5. Ready in 4–8 weeks when cool, earthy, and crumbly.

### Sheet Composting (No-Turn)

1. Spread browns and greens directly on the soil.
2. Cover with mulch.
3. Worms and microbes do the work over 6–12 months.

### Trench Composting

1. Dig a 30 cm trench.
2. Bury kitchen scraps.
3. Cover with soil.
4. Plant above after 1 month.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Smells rotten | Too wet, no air | Turn, add browns |
| Not heating up | Too dry, not enough greens | Water, add greens |
| Attracts pests | Meat/dairy in pile | Bury deep, omit these |

## Safety Notes

- Do not compost meat, dairy, or pet waste in open piles.
- Hot compost kills pathogens; cold compost does not.
- Wash hands after handling.

title: Crop Rotation
materialsRequired: Map of plots
Seeds for 4 families
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Rotation breaks pest cycles, balances nutrients, and prevents soil depletion.
Rule: never plant the same family in the same bed two years in a row.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Map of plots
- Seeds for 4 families

## Procedure

### The Four-Family Rotation

| Year | Bed 1 | Bed 2 | Bed 3 | Bed 4 |
|------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 1 | Legume | Brassica | Root | Fruiting |
| 2 | Brassica | Root | Fruiting | Legume |
| 3 | Root | Fruiting | Legume | Brassica |
| 4 | Fruiting | Legume | Brassica | Root |

Families:

- **Legume:** pea, bean, clover — fixes nitrogen
- **Brassica:** cabbage, broccoli, kale — heavy feeder
- **Root:** carrot, beet, onion — loosens soil
- **Fruiting:** tomato, pepper, squash — heavy feeder

### Cover Crops

- Winter: rye, vetch, clover
- Summer: buckwheat, cowpea
- Chop and till in before seed set to add organic matter.

### Fallow

- Rest a bed every 4 years.
- Plant with a legume cover and let it mature.

## Safety Notes

- Do not rotate tomatoes with potatoes (same family, shared diseases).
- Do not follow a legume with another legume.

title: Food Preservation
materialsRequired: Drying rack
Salt
Glass jars with lids
Smokehouse
Root cellar

sources.title: USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Preservation extends harvest into winter. Methods: drying, salting, smoking,
canning, fermenting, and root cellaring.

## Prerequisites

- [Making Fire](../survival/making-fire.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Drying rack
- Salt
- Glass jars with lids
- Smokehouse
- Root cellar

## Procedure

### Sun Drying

1. Slice food 3–6 mm thick.
2. Lay on a rack in full sun, covered with mesh.
3. Turn daily; dry 2–5 days until leathery.
4. Rehydrate in water before use.

### Salting

1. Layer food with coarse salt (1 kg salt per 4 kg food).
2. Weight down; keep submerged in brine.
3. Ready in 2–6 weeks.
4. Rinse before eating.

### Smoking

1. Build a small fire in a smokehouse.
2. Use hardwood (hickory, oak, apple). Never resinous softwoods.
3. Cold smoke (20–30°C) for 1–3 days for preservation.
4. Hot smoke (60–80°C) for immediate consumption.

### Water-Bath Canning (High-Acid Foods)

1. Sterilize jars in boiling water.
2. Fill with hot food, leaving 1 cm headspace.
3. Seal; process in boiling water for the recipe time.
4. Cool; check seal (lid should not flex).

### Pressure Canning (Low-Acid Foods)

1. Use a pressure canner at 10 PSI (115°C) for low-acid foods (meat, beans).
2. Water-bath canning does **not** kill botulism spores.

### Fermenting

1. Submerge vegetables in 2% brine.
2. Keep anaerobic; weight down.
3. Ferment 1–4 weeks at 18–22°C.
4. Refrigerate when sour to taste.

### Root Cellaring

1. Ideal: 0–4°C, 90–95% humidity, dark.
2. Store root vegetables in sand or straw.
3. Ventilate to prevent ethylene buildup.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Botulism from improperly canned low-acid foods is often fatal.
- Discard any can with bulging lid, off-smell, or cloudiness.
- Boil all home-canned low-acid food for 10 minutes before eating.

title: Grain Cultivation
materialsRequired: Seed grain
Plow or hoe
Sickle or scythe
Threshing surface
Winnowing basket
Mill (see [Mills](../materials/mills.md))
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Grains (wheat, rice, maize, barley, millet) provide the calorie base of
civilization. They store dry for years.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)
- [Crop Rotation](crop-rotation.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Seed grain
- Plow or hoe
- Sickle or scythe
- Threshing surface
- Winnowing basket
- Mill (see [Mills](../materials/mills.md))

## Procedure

### Soil Preparation

1. Test soil; amend with compost to pH 6–7.
2. Plow to 15–20 cm.
3. Harrow to break clods.

### Sowing

1. Broadcast or drill seed at the rate for your grain:
   - Wheat: 100–150 kg/ha
   - Rice (transplanted): 40–60 kg/ha
   - Maize: 20–25 kg/ha
2. Cover lightly with soil.

### Growing

1. Water: 400–650 mm per season for wheat; rice needs flooding.
2. Weed at 3 weeks and 6 weeks.
3. Watch for rust, blight, and locusts.

### Harvest

1. Cut when grain is hard and heads nod.
2. Bundle into shocks; dry in the field 1–2 weeks.
3. Thresh by beating bundles on a hard surface.
4. Winnow by tossing in the wind.

### Storage

1. Dry grain to <12% moisture (bites crack, not dent).
2. Store in airtight containers with desiccant.
3. Add diatomaceous earth to prevent weevils.
4. Cool, dark, dry place. Viability: 5–20 years.

## Safety Notes

- Ergot (fungal infection of rye) is toxic — discard black grains.
- Grain dust is explosive; ventilate threshing areas.
- Rice paddies breed mosquitoes; manage standing water.

title: Grain Storage and Pest Control
yield: A 1 m3 bin holds roughly 600-800 kg of dry grain
season: Immediately after harvest; cool, dry grain stores best
storage: Dry to 12-14% moisture; 6-24 months in hermetic or well-sealed storage
hazards: Mould and aflatoxin from damp grain
Dust explosion and fumigant poisoning
Bin collapse or engulfment
Rodents, insects, and birds
materialsRequired: Raised, sealed bin or hermetic bags
Moisture meter
Clean tarps
Diatomaceous earth
Pallets
Rodent-proof mesh
Labels
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Grain that is stored wet or warm can lose a season's work to mould, insects,
and rodents in weeks. The two decisive variables are moisture and temperature:
dry grain below about 12-14% moisture, kept cool and sealed, stores for 6-24
months. A 1 m³ bin holds roughly 600-800 kg of grain.

## Prerequisites

- Grain cultivation and harvesting
- A dry, raised storage site

## Materials & Tools

- Raised, sealed bin or hermetic storage bags
- Moisture meter
- Clean tarps and pallets
- Diatomaceous earth
- Rodent-proof mesh
- Labels and a record book

## Procedure

### 1. Harvest and dry

1. Harvest at maturity and avoid mixing wet or mouldy grain with good grain.
2. Dry to 12-14% moisture; test with a moisture meter, not by bite.
3. Dry on clean tarps, in thin layers, with airflow and sun.
4. Cool the grain before storage; warm grain sweats as it cools.

### 2. Clean and prepare the store

1. Winnow or sieve out chaff, broken kernels, and dust.
2. Clean the bin, remove old grain, and repair holes and gaps.
3. Raise the bin off the floor and keep it away from walls.
4. Fit rodent mesh over vents and keep the lid sealed.

### 3. Fill and protect

1. Fill the bin in one session and level the surface.
2. Use hermetic bags for small quantities; seal them fully.
3. Mix diatomaceous earth at the label rate for insect control where approved.
4. Label each lot with the harvest date and moisture reading.

### 4. Monitor and treat

1. Check monthly for warmth, condensation, insects, or rodent droppings.
2. Probe the centre and bottom; a hot spot means mould or insects.
3. Remove and use affected grain first; do not mix it with clean grain.
4. Fumigate only with trained help and approved products; never in a living
   space.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Mouldy grain can contain aflatoxins that cause liver
  damage and cancer. Do not eat or feed visibly mouldy grain.
- Grain dust can explode. Ventilate, avoid open flames, and wear a mask when
  cleaning.
- Fumigants are highly toxic. Use only with training, respirators, and warning
  signs.
- Never enter a grain bin that may have bridged; engulfment can kill in
  seconds.

title: Irrigation Scheduling
yield: A written irrigation schedule that refills the root zone with measured applications and avoids runoff
season: Adjust weekly during the growing season; reduce or stop at harvest and dormancy
storage: Store drip tape and fittings dry and out of sunlight between seasons
hazards: Drowning in ditches, ponds, and tanks
Slips on wet paths and buried pipes
Electric shock from pumps and controls
Crop contamination from unsafe water

resourceBudget.batch: 100 square metres of vegetable bed for one week

lifespan: Recalibrate the schedule each season and whenever the crop stage changes
maintenance: Check emitters and filters weekly; flush lines monthly
limits: Scheduling figures are crop, soil, and climate specific
Do not use untreated sewage or industrial water on edible crops
Do not irrigate steep slopes faster than the soil can absorb

sources.title: UC ANR Irrigation Scheduling for Small Farms

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Irrigation scheduling replaces habit with measurement: water when the root zone
is approaching its limit, apply enough to refill it, and stop before runoff.
Overwatering wastes fuel and nutrients and can drown roots; underwatering
reduces yield even when leaves look healthy. A moisture test, a known application
rate, and a simple log are enough to improve most small plots.

## Prerequisites

- A reliable water source and storage
- Basic soil and crop knowledge

## Materials & Tools

- Soil auger or digging trowel
- Moisture meter or tensiometers
- Catch cans or graduated containers
- Flow meter, timer, or calibrated bucket
- Drip tape, emitters, or furrow gates
- Mulch
- Notebook and rain gauge

## Procedure

### 1. Measure the soil and the application rate

1. Dig 15-30 cm down and squeeze a handful of soil; crumbly and slightly damp
   is workable, while dry dust or free water indicates a problem.
2. Use a moisture meter or tensiometer at root depth and record readings at the
   same time each day.
3. Measure how long the system takes to deliver 10 mm of water using catch cans
   or a flow meter.
4. Map the plot into zones with similar soil, slope, and crop stage.

### 2. Set a water budget

1. Estimate crop water use from local evapotranspiration data or a reference
   crop chart; adjust for sun, wind, and crop stage.
2. Subtract effective rainfall recorded by the rain gauge.
3. Apply water to refill the root zone, not to wet the surface every day.
4. Keep a simple ledger of date, zone, millimetres applied, and rainfall.

### 3. Apply water efficiently

1. Irrigate early morning or evening to reduce evaporation and wind loss.
2. Use drip or furrow systems that deliver water to roots rather than leaves.
3. Alternate wet and dry cycles where crops allow; this discourages some
   diseases and saves water.
4. Stop when water begins to run off or when the root zone is refilled.

### 4. Maintain and adjust

1. Flush drip lines and clean filters weekly; check emitters for clogging.
2. Repair leaks and reset timers after power or pressure changes.
3. Mulch beds to slow evaporation and keep soil temperature stable.
4. Recheck the schedule after thinning, harvest, or a change in weather.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Wet soil, ponds, and irrigation ditches are drowning and
  fall hazards, especially for children.
- Do not irrigate with untreated sewage or industrial water on edible crops.
- Slippery paths and buried pipes can cause falls and injuries.
- Pumps and electrical controls must be grounded and kept out of floodwater.

title: Raising Livestock
materialsRequired: Fencing
Feed (grain, hay, forage)
Water source
Shelter
Veterinary basics (see [Health](../health/README.md))
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Livestock convert grass and waste into protein, fat, leather, and fertilizer.
Start small — chickens and rabbits first, then goats or pigs, then cattle.

## Prerequisites

- [Composting](composting.md)
- [Emergency Shelter](../survival/emergency-shelter.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Fencing
- Feed (grain, hay, forage)
- Water source
- Shelter
- Veterinary basics (see [Health](../health/README.md))

## Procedure

### Chickens

1. Coop: 0.4 m² per bird, roosts 30 cm off ground.
2. Feed: 100 g layer pellets per bird per day + forage.
3. Water: 250 mL per bird per day.
4. Eggs: 1 per hen per day in peak season.
5. Slaughter at 18–24 months for stewing hens.

### Rabbits

1. Hutch: 0.5 m² per adult.
2. Feed: hay ad libitum, 100 g pellets, greens.
3. Breeding: 1 buck per 10 does; gestation 30 days.
4. Yield: 4–8 kg meat per year per doe.

### Goats (Dairy)

1. Shelter: 2 m² per goat, dry bedding.
2. Feed: browse + 1 kg hay + 0.5 kg grain per day.
3. Milk: 2–4 L per day, twice daily.
4. Breeding: seasonal; gestation 150 days.

### Pigs

1. Pen: 10 m² per pig.
2. Feed: kitchen waste, grain, forage.
3. Farrowing: 1 litter per year, 8–12 piglets.
4. Slaughter at 6–8 months (100 kg).

### Cattle

1. Pasture: 0.4–1 ha per cow.
2. Feed: grass/hay + minerals.
3. Milk: 15–30 L/day for dairy breeds.
4. Breeding: 1 bull per 30 cows; gestation 280 days.

### Health Basics

- Quarantine new animals 2 weeks.
- Vaccinate per local disease profile.
- Deworm quarterly.
- Isolate sick animals immediately.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Zoonotic diseases (brucellosis, rabies, salmonella)
  transmit from animals.
- Always wash hands after handling.
- Bulls and boars can be aggressive; never turn your back.
- Slaughter humanely; stun before bleeding.

title: Seed Saving
materialsRequired: Healthy plants (select best specimens)
Cloth bags
Glass jars
Silica desiccant
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Saved seed preserves genetic diversity and independence. Open-pollinated
(heirloom) varieties breed true; hybrids do not.

## Prerequisites

- [Soil Testing](soil-testing.md)
- [Crop Rotation](crop-rotation.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Healthy plants (select best specimens)
- Cloth bags
- Glass jars
- Silica desiccant

## Procedure

### Self-Pollinating (Tomato, Bean, Pea, Lettuce)

1. Let fruits mature fully on the plant.
2. For tomatoes: ferment seeds in water 3 days to remove gel.
3. Rinse, dry on a plate (not paper towel).
4. Store in a cool, dark, dry place.

### Cross-Pollinating (Corn, Squash, Brassicas)

1. Isolate varieties by 400 m or use hand-pollination.
2. Bag unopened flowers; hand-pollinate with a brush.
3. Re-bag until fruit sets.

### Biennials (Carrot, Onion, Cabbage)

1. Overwinter roots/bulbs.
2. Replant in spring.
3. Harvest seed heads when dry.

### Storage

1. Dry seeds to <10% moisture (they snap, not bend).
2. Store in glass jars with desiccant.
3. Label: species, variety, year, source.
4. Cool (5–10°C), dark, dry. Viability: 3–10 years.

## Safety Notes

- Do not save seed from diseased plants.
- Do not save seed from F1 hybrids.
- Label meticulously — misidentified seed is worse than no seed.

title: Soil Fertility Management
yield: A soil-fertility plan with tested amendments, organic matter, and a rotation that maintains yield
season: Sample after harvest; apply compost and lime before the main planting window
storage: Cover compost and fertilizer stacks; keep lime dry and labelled
hazards: Pathogens in fresh manure
Dust and chemical irritation from lime and fertilizer
Nitrate and phosphorus runoff into water
Heavy-metal contamination from untested inputs
lifespan: Expect 3-5 years to rebuild depleted organic matter and structure
maintenance: Test soil every 2-3 years and add compost or cover crops each season
limits: Do not lime without a pH test
Do not use fresh manure on crops eaten raw
Do not spread amendments before heavy rain or near wells and streams
materialsRequired: Mature compost or rotted manure
Cover crop seed
Lime or gypsum only if tested
Mulch
Soil sample bags

sources.title: Cornell Comprehensive Assessment of Soil Health

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Fertility is not just nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. It is organic matter,
soil structure, pH, and a living community of roots and microbes. Feed the soil
with compost, cover crops, and balanced minerals, and most crops need fewer
external inputs. Test before adding amendments; guessing at lime or manure rates
can create deficiencies, salinity, or polluted water.

## Prerequisites

- Composting or access to mature compost
- Basic crop rotation knowledge

## Materials & Tools

- Soil test results or a field test kit
- Mature compost or well-rotted manure
- Cover crop seed
- Agricultural lime or gypsum only if indicated
- Mulch and erosion-control fabric
- Spade, hoe, and wheelbarrow
- Soil auger and sample bags

## Procedure

### 1. Sample and assess

1. Divide the plot into zones with similar soil, slope, and cropping history.
2. Take 10-15 cores from each zone at 0-20 cm depth, mix them, and send a
   composite sample to a laboratory.
3. Record pH, organic matter, phosphorus, potassium, and any micronutrients
   flagged by the lab.
4. Note drainage, compaction, erosion, and earthworm activity in a field log.

### 2. Build organic matter

1. Apply 2-5 cm of mature compost to beds and incorporate it shallowly.
2. Grow cover crops in the off-season: legumes for nitrogen, grasses for
   biomass, and deep-rooted species for compaction.
3. Keep soil covered with mulch or living plants to protect structure and
   moisture.
4. Avoid burning crop residues; compost or incorporate them instead.

### 3. Correct pH and minerals

1. Apply lime only when the test calls for it; over-liming locks up
   micronutrients.
2. Use gypsum for sodic or compacted soils only after confirming the problem.
3. Add phosphorus and potassium according to crop removal and soil test levels.
4. Re-test after one or two seasons rather than adding more blindly.

### 4. Rotate and protect

1. Rotate plant families to interrupt pests and diseases and balance nutrient
   demand.
2. Include a legume at least every third season where climate allows.
3. Keep rows across the slope, maintain grass waterways, and avoid working wet
   soil.
4. Record yields and amendments so the next season can adjust the plan.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Manure and compost can carry pathogens. Use well-rotted
  material on food crops and wash produce.
- Lime and fertilizer dust irritate eyes and lungs; wear gloves, eye protection,
  and a dust mask.
- Do not spread manure or fertilizer before heavy rain or near wells and
  streams.
- Soil tests from contaminated sites need laboratory analysis for heavy metals.

title: Soil Testing
materialsRequired: Jar with lid
Vinegar
Baking soda
Distilled water
Shovel
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Soil health determines crop yield. Test pH, texture, and organic matter
before planting.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Jar with lid
- Vinegar
- Baking soda
- Distilled water
- Shovel

## Procedure

### Jar Test (Texture)

1. Fill a jar ⅓ with soil, top with water, add a pinch of detergent.
2. Shake vigorously for 3 minutes.
3. Let settle 24 hours.
4. Measure layers: sand (bottom), silt, clay (top). Ratios indicate loam, sandy,
   or clay.

### pH Test (Vinegar & Baking Soda)

1. Place 2 tbsp soil in a cup.
2. Add vinegar. If it fizzes → alkaline (pH > 7).
3. If no fizz, repeat with baking soda + water. Fizz → acidic (pH < 7).
4. No reaction either way → neutral (pH ~7).

### Organic Matter Test

1. Weigh a dry soil sample.
2. Burn it in a fire-safe container until only ash remains.
3. Weight loss = organic matter content. Aim for 5%.

### Drainage Test

1. Dig a 30 cm hole; fill with water.
2. Refill after it drains. Measure time to drain second fill.
3. 2–4 cm/hour is ideal.

## Safety Notes

- Vinegar/baking soda reactions are harmless but messy.
- Burning soil releases smoke; do outdoors.

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Keeping livestock means managing breeding, feeding, health, and records so
that the herd works for the household. Genetics sets what an animal can do;
the environment decides how much of that it shows. The key principle: what
you measure, you can select for, and what you do not record, you cannot
improve.

## Prerequisites

- Basic animal care and safe handling experience
- A breeding stock and a herd book or spreadsheet
- A feed table for the species and the local forage
- A relationship with a veterinarian who will visit the farm

## Materials & Tools

- Breeding animals of the chosen breed or cross
- Scales or a weight tape for recording live weight
- Marking tags, ear notches, or a tattoo kit
- Pedigree and performance ledger
- Handling pens, a race, and a safe squeeze chute for larger stock
- Feed, forage, and mineral supplements matched to the species

## Procedure

### Defining the Goal

1. List the traits that matter, such as live weight gain, litter size,
   milk yield, meat yield, or docility.
2. Rank them by the value they add and set a measurement for each one.
3. Establish the flock or herd average before selecting anything, so that
   later improvement can be shown.

### Choosing a Mating System

1. Use purebred mating to fix a known set of traits, and expect the
   inbreeding coefficient to rise by about 1 percent per generation in a
   closed population.
2. Use crossbreeding where hybrid vigour matters; first crosses commonly
   gain 3 to 5 percent in growth over the parent breeds.
3. Backcross the best offspring to the parent breed to keep most of the
   improved genetics, replacing about half the genome each generation.
4. Avoid mating close relatives, and bring in new breeding stock from
   outside the herd every few years.

### Recording and Selecting

1. Record every birth with both parent identifications, the date, and the
   number born.
2. Weigh animals at a fixed age, such as weaning and yearling, so the
   comparison is fair.
3. Estimate heritability from your own records; milk yield in cattle sits
    near 0.3, while litter size in pigs sits near 0.1 to 0.15.
4. Keep only the animals that meet the standard as parents, and cull
    animals with repeated structural faults, poor udders, or chronic
    lameness.
5. Expect the response to selection to be about the heritability times the
    selection differential, check the real gain each year, and plan mating
    calendars around the species: about 283 days of gestation in cattle,
    114 days in pigs, and 147 to 152 days in sheep.

## Safety Notes

- Large animals can crush, kick, and trample; work from a protected
  position, keep the escape route clear, and never stand directly behind an
  animal.
- Handling a boar, a bull, or a mare with a foal is high risk; use
  barriers and experienced handlers.
- Several animal diseases cross to people, including ringworm, tetanus,
  brucellosis, and rabies; wash hands, wear gloves for calving, and keep
  vaccination records current.
- Feed that has moulded or been stored damp can cause mycotoxicosis; never
  feed material that smells sour or shows fuzz.
- Keep young children out of animal pens, and never leave a child alone
  with livestock of any size.
- Use a proper handling facility rather than improvising with rope and
  gates, and wear boots that can be washed and disinfected.

## Overview

Aseptic technique keeps unwanted microbes out of cultures that must stay
clean, and keeps unknown microbes contained while you work with them. It is
the foundation under diagnostics, food testing, and every starter culture.
The key principle: sterilise everything that touches the medium, and never
open a vessel near your face.

## Prerequisites

- Training in laboratory safety and in biosafety levels
- A working autoclave, or access to one
- A laminar flow cabinet or a clean bench
- Instruction in handling cultures of unknown identity

## Materials & Tools

- Autoclave with a validated cycle and indicator tape
- Pressure cooker usable as a fallback steriliser
- Laminar flow cabinet or still clean bench
- Heat-resistant gloves, apron, and closed shoes
- Culture vessels with loose or vented lids, and an inoculating loop
- Media: nutrient broth and nutrient agar, plus selective media
- Sterile petri dishes, a 0.1 millilitre pipette, and a colony counter
- Incubator or cabinet held at 30 to 37 degrees C
- 70 percent ethanol, or isopropanol, and a surface disinfectant

## Procedure

### Preparing and Sterilising

1. Clean the bench and wipe it with disinfectant before every session, then
   wrap the instruments and media and label each batch with its contents
   and the date.
2. Sterilise liquids in the autoclave at 121 degrees C for 15 minutes at
   about 103 kilopascals, using a validated liquid cycle; never autoclave a
   sealed container.
3. Sterilise glassware and instruments dry at 160 degrees C for 2 hours, or
   at 121 degrees C for 30 minutes on a wrapped cycle.
4. Open the autoclave only once the pressure gauge reads zero and the
   indicator tape or printout confirms the cycle.
5. Cool sterile medium to 45 to 50 degrees C before pouring plates, then
   set the poured plates down lid-side down.

### Transferring Culture

1. Work in the cabinet with the sash low, flame the loop until it glows,
   and let it cool for 5 to 10 seconds before touching the culture.
2. Open vessels as briefly as possible, keep the cap in your hand, never
   talk over an open plate, and close plates promptly.
3. Keep agar surfaces moist by stacking the plates face to face.

### Isolating and Counting Colonies

1. Streak a loopful across the plate in four overlapping quadrants so that
   single colonies are separated.
2. Incubate the plates upside down at 30 to 37 degrees C and read them
    after 18 to 48 hours.
3. Prepare serial tenfold dilutions, from 10 to the minus 1 up to 10 to
    the minus 7, and plate 0.1 millilitre from two or three dilutions onto
    duplicate plates.
4. Count only the plates that hold between 30 and 300 colonies, average
    the duplicates, then multiply the mean count by the dilution factor and
    by 10 to obtain colony forming units per millilitre.

## Safety Notes

- Cultures of unknown identity may contain pathogens; treat every culture
  as potentially hazardous and handle it at the correct biosafety level
  under a supervisor.
- Sterilising pressure vessels can rupture; never autoclave a sealed
  container and never open the door until the gauge reads zero.
- Flames, hot medium, and melted agar cause burns; keep flammables away
  and let agar cool before handling it.
- Ethanol is flammable and its vapour ignites readily; let it fully
  evaporate before using any flame nearby.
- Broken glass and contaminated sharps cause lacerations; put them in
  puncture-proof containers, never in the general waste.
- Disinfectants and antibiotics can sensitise skin; wear gloves and wash
  after every session.

## Overview

Every living thing is built from cells, and a microscope turns an opaque smear
of tissue into visible structure. Knowing cell structure and preparing slides
well is the difference between seeing bacteria and seeing only stained debris.
The key principle is that most specimens are transparent, so contrast has to
come from stains, from phase contrast, or from the optics of the instrument.

## Prerequisites

- Safe use of a compound light microscope
- Making a simple wet mount
- Handling a specimen without contaminating it or yourself

## Materials & Tools

- Compound light microscope with 4x, 10x, 40x, and 100x objectives, a
  movable stage, and a lamp
- Slides, cover slips, a dropper, and a lens tissue
- Methylene blue or crystal violet stain, dilute iodine, and India ink
- Cotton swabs, toothpicks, and sterile sample swabs
- Covered containers for specimens, and gloves
- Immersion oil for the 100x objective
- Hand lens of 10x for a gross look before you mount anything
- Notebook for drawings and counts

## Procedure

### Stage 1: Set up and focus the microscope

1. Place the microscope on a stable bench with the lamp at the back and the
   objectives turned away from you.
2. Switch on the lamp, raise the stage, and bring the 4x objective into
   position over the specimen.
3. Move the slide until the specimen is in the lit area, focus with the coarse
   knob and then the fine knob, then centre the specimen and step up through
   10x to 40x, raising the lamp brightness as you go.

### Stage 2: Prepare a wet mount

1. Place a drop of water on a clean slide and use a swab or toothpick to take a
   very small amount of the sample.
2. Stir the sample gently in the drop to spread it, then lower a cover slip at
   an angle so the air is pushed out rather than trapped.
3. Add one drop of stain at the edge of the cover slip and draw it through
   with blotting paper on the opposite side.

### Stage 3: Show specific structures

1. To reveal nuclei and cell walls, use methylene blue at about 0.1 percent
   and stain for 60 seconds; for starch and other granules, use dilute
   iodine, which turns blue-black where starch is present.
2. For a negative stain, mix a dilute cell suspension with India ink and
   observe the unstained cells as bright shapes against a dark ground.

### Stage 4: Record what you see

1. Draw the field of view at 400x and mark the scale bar, or the measured
   field diameter for that objective.
2. Note the arrangement of the cells, whether a cell wall is present, and
   whether the cells are moving, then repeat on a fresh sample.

### Stage 5: Care for the instrument

1. Lower the stage fully, remove the slide, and wipe each objective with lens
   tissue after use.
2. Cover the microscope, switch off the lamp, and store it in a dry case.

## Safety Notes

- Never look down the eyepiece while raising the stage or swinging an
  objective in. It will drive the slide into your eye.
- The 100x objective needs immersion oil. Use it only with the correct
  cover slip, and wipe the oil off afterwards or it will gum up the optics.
- Microscope lamps get hot and can scorch paper and benches. Keep the
  instrument on a stable, clear surface.
- Use a fresh slide and a fresh swab for every specimen so you do not spread
  contamination between samples.
- Handle clinical or unknown biological specimens with gloves, and only with
  appropriate training, supervision, and equipment. Do not eat or drink at
  the bench.
- Do not incubate or grow unknown material in an open room. Work with a
  supervisor and follow the site's containment rules.

## Overview

Biodiversity is judged on repeatability, not on one good survey. Fixed
plots, consistent timing, and honest counts are what let you show change
across years. The key principle: if you change the method, the numbers
stop being comparable, so change the method only deliberately and record
it.

## Prerequisites

- A clear question, such as which habitat is losing species fastest
- Permission to enter the land, and a local guide to its species
- A written survey protocol with fixed dates and plot codes

## Materials & Tools

- A measuring tape or a fixed transect line marked at intervals
- A quadrat frame of 0.5 m by 0.5 m or 1 m by 1 m
- A clipboard and waterproof data forms
- A camera with a date stamp for repeatable photographs
- A species identification guide for the region
- A hand lens and a 10x loupe
- A GPS receiver, or a phone with offline maps
- A compass, a slope meter, and a mallet and posts for marking plots
- A brush for cleaning the quadrat between samples

## Procedure

### Design the Survey

1. Choose one indicator species group and one habitat to survey first, and
   decide the sample size before starting; 20 to 30 plots is a workable
   minimum.
2. Mark permanent plots with a post and a unique code, and record the
   coordinates, elevation, slope, and aspect of every plot.
3. Set a survey window so that all plots are sampled in the same two weeks
   each year.
4. Decide who counts what, so two observers record the same things.

### Count at Each Plot

1. Arrive at the plot and record the date, the time, and the observer,
   then walk the transect or place the quadrat at the marked intervals.
2. Count each plant species in the quadrat, or estimate percent cover.
3. Count animals by sight, by sound, or with a net, within a fixed time of
   effort.
4. Photograph the plot from the same fixed points every visit, note
   disturbance, grazing, fire damage, and illegal activity, and clean the
   quadrat before moving on.

### Analyse and Report

1. Sum the counts for each species across all plots.
2. Calculate the Shannon index, H equals minus the sum of p times the
   natural log of p, where p is each species' share of the total.
3. Calculate the Simpson index as one minus the sum of the squared shares,
   and compare both indices against the previous year.
4. Report the raw counts beside the indices, and record every change of
   method as a break in the series.

## Safety Notes

- Tell someone your route, the plot codes, and your expected return time.
- Carry a charged phone, a paper map, and a compass, because maps fail
  without signal.
- Wear closed shoes in long grass and watch for snakes, scorpions, and
  stinging plants.
- Stay off unstable ground and away from slips and bogs during and after
  rain.
- Do not remove, disturb, or collect the organisms you are counting.
- Keep off private, fenced, mining, and military land without permission.

## Overview

Enzymes are biological catalysts that make reactions fast enough to be
useful, and the bacteria and yeasts that use them turn sugar into food,
drink, and useful chemicals. Control of temperature, pH, and time decides
which organism wins and what it makes. The key principle: a ferment is a
controlled culture, and an uncontrolled one is a spoilage risk.

## Prerequisites

- A basic understanding of acids, bases, and pH
- Clean glass jars with lids that seal but can vent gas
- A thermometer and pH strips or an indicator

## Materials & Tools

- Sugar source: honey, molasses, fruit, milk, or grain
- Starter culture: baker's yeast, live yoghurt culture, or sourdough
- Salt, and herbs or spices for flavour
- Clean jars, a weight to hold the lids down, and a straining cloth
- Thermometer, pH strips, and a hydrometer for liquid brews

## Procedure

### Understanding Enzyme Behaviour

1. Name the substrate, the enzyme, and the product for the process you
   care about.
2. Measure the rate by following change in pH, temperature, or product
   over time.
3. Raise the temperature by 10 degrees C and expect the rate to roughly
   double, until the enzyme denatures and the rate falls away.
4. Hold the pH within a couple of units of the enzyme optimum, near pH 2
   for pepsin and near pH 8 for trypsin.
5. Stop the reaction by heating the mixture to 70 to 80 degrees C once the
   product is made.

### Running a Starter Culture

1. Dissolve the sugar in water at about 10 to 20 percent by weight, then
   bring the mixture to the starting temperature of the culture: 35 degrees
   C for bread yeast, 42 to 46 degrees C for yoghurt, and 18 to 25 degrees
   C for most lactic cultures.
2. Add the starter at 5 to 20 percent of the volume, stir it in, and hold
   it closed to the air for as long as the culture needs.
3. Allow 4 to 8 hours for yoghurt and 4 to 12 hours for a sourdough rise,
   judging progress by taste and smell rather than by the clock alone.

### Preserving the Product

1. Salt vegetables at 2 percent by weight and hold them under the brine for
   2 to 4 weeks.
2. Check that the brine has dropped below pH 4.0, by titration or pH
    strip, before the jar is stored.
3. Refrigerate the finished food, or keep it sealed in a cool place below
    15 degrees C.
4. Save a portion of the starter as the next inoculum, and label it with
    the date and the crop it was used on.

## Safety Notes

- Low-acid anaerobic foods, including home-canned vegetables and fish, can
  carry Clostridium botulinum spores whose toxin is odourless and tasteless;
  only eat food that was pressure-canned or acidified to pH 4.6 or below.
- Ferments can produce methanol and other higher alcohols; keep distillation
  equipment away from open flames and never ferment in a sealed container.
- A fermenting mash releases carbon dioxide; never seal it airtight, and
  open it away from your face because the gas can cause pressure injury.
- Mould on the surface of a ferment can carry toxins; discard the whole
  batch rather than skimming the top off.
- Wash hands and utensils between batches so that spoilage organisms are
  not carried from one ferment into the next.
- Keep cultures away from children and animals, and never use utensils
  that also handle raw meat.

## Overview

Fresh water carries a food web that runs from algae and bacteria up to
fish, birds, and people. Water quality sets the ceiling on that food web,
and dissolved oxygen is usually the first thing to fail. The key principle:
cold, well-oxygenated water with low nutrient input sustains far more life
than warm, stagnant, enriched water.

## Prerequisites

- Water Quality Testing
- A working knowledge of local rivers, lakes, and their seasonal cycles
- Basic arithmetic with concentrations and units

## Materials & Tools

- Dissolved oxygen meter, or a Winkler titration kit with a burette
- A thermometer reading to 0.1 degrees C
- A pH meter, or a colour comparison kit
- A Secchi disk of 30 to 40 cm on a marked line
- One litre sample bottles with tight caps, and a cooler
- A turbidity tube and a conductivity meter
- A kick net, sorting trays, and a magnifier
- Nitrate and phosphate field test kits
- A field data sheet, one row per station and date

## Procedure

### Survey the Site

1. Fix each sampling station with a marker and a permanent code, and
   record its coordinates.
2. Sample upstream, at the site itself, and downstream of it.
3. Work the same stations in the same season every year, and record the
   time, the weather, and recent rainfall at every visit.

### Measure Water Quality

1. Fill the dissolved oxygen bottle with no trapped air, because a single
   bubble biases the reading low.
2. Measure temperature at the same depth every time, read dissolved
   oxygen in mg/L, and correct the reading for temperature.
3. Measure pH in the field, then conductivity and turbidity, run nitrate
   and phosphate tests on a filtered, chilled sample, and record clarity
   with a Secchi disk.

### Sample the Food Web

1. Kick the bottom substrate upstream of the net at each station.
2. Sort the catch and count the organisms by group, then count the algae
   and rooted plants in a 0.1 square metre quadrat.
3. Note pollution signs such as foam, odour, algal mats, and dead fish,
   then walk upstream to find the source of the loading.

### Interpret and Report

1. Compare each station with the reference station upstream of it.
2. Flag dissolved oxygen below 5 mg/L as a stress signal; saturated water
   at 20 degrees C holds only about 9 mg/L.
3. Flag nitrate above 10 mg/L as nutrient enrichment, plot every
   parameter against date, and publish the sheet each year, including the
   results that showed no change.

## Safety Notes

- Work from stable banks and wear a buoyancy aid; cold water and current
  pull people in without warning.
- Do not wade in deep or fast channels, and avoid flooded channels after
  rain.
- Handle wastewater samples with gloves and wash hands before eating.
- Keep sample bottles clean; a dirty bottle ruins a trace nutrient result.
- Never swim downstream of a suspected sewage or chemical discharge.
- Cover cuts and any skin abrasions, because standing water can carry
  leptospirosis and other pathogens.

## Overview

Fungi recycle dead matter into soil and trade minerals for plant sugars
through mycorrhizal partnerships at the root. The mushroom is only the
fruiting body; the organism is the mycelium spreading through the soil.
The key principle: learn the mycelium, not just the cap, because that is
the part doing the work.

## Prerequisites

- Soil Biology and Composting
- A local guide to the edible and poisonous fungi of the region
- Basic plant identification, to link fungi to their host trees

## Materials & Tools

- A hand lens of 10x and a printed field guide
- A camera, for photographs of the cap, stem, and gills in place
- A small knife and a clean board for cutting specimens
- White and black paper, a glass slide, a cup, and a bowl for spore prints
- A microscope at 400x for measuring spores
- Plastic bags and a marker for separating individual collections
- A hand trowel for soil sampling around the roots of a host tree
- Leaf mould and wood chips for mulching mycorrhizal plantings

## Procedure

### Identify a Specimen Safely

1. Photograph the specimen in place, including the cap, the stem base, and
   any ring or volva.
2. Record the substrate, the nearby trees, the date, and the gill
   attachment: free, attached, notched, or descending.
3. Compare every feature against the guide, including the spore print
   colour, before anything is eaten.

### Take a Spore Print

1. Remove the cap and lay it gills-down on white and black paper, or on a
   glass slide, then cover it with a bowl.
2. Leave it undisturbed for 6 to 12 hours in still, humid air.
3. Lift the cap and the paper together, read the print colour in daylight,
   and measure the spores under 400x if a microscope is available.

### Harvest for Food

1. Cut the specimen cleanly at the base, leave the mycelium in the ground,
   and take less than a third of what you can see.
2. Keep each collection in its own bag, because one poisonous cap spoils a
   basket.
3. Cook thoroughly, never eat a wild mushroom raw, and learn the two or
   three edible species that grow near you before widening the search.

### Maintain Mycorrhizal Associations

1. Plant host species that suit both the climate and the local fungal
   community, and keep the root zone planted and undisturbed.
2. Avoid deep tilling, which severs the hyphae that feed the roots, and
   skip high-phosphorus fertiliser, which suppresses the partnership.
3. Mulch with leaf litter or wood chips to feed the fungi, and spread
   spore-bearing mulch from a healthy stand onto bare ground.

## Safety Notes

- Mushroom poisoning is a medical emergency; keep the specimen so it can be
  identified, and seek medical help at once.
- Never taste a wild mushroom to test it; taste tests are how people die.
- Confusion between edible and deadly look-alikes is common, so treat any
  uncertain cap as poisonous.
- Spores from old, dried, or mouldy specimens can trigger respiratory
  allergy; do not inhale them.
- Some species irritate skin and gut; wash hands and do not handle spoiled
  or rotting material bare-handed.
- Do not collect where spray or herbicide has been used, or within the
  required buffer of roadsides and treated land.

## Overview

Immunity has two layers: innate defence, which acts within minutes, and
adaptive defence, which is slower but remembers. Vaccination trains the
adaptive layer so the body meets a pathogen faster and milder. The key
principle: a vaccine that has broken its cold chain is not a weaker
vaccine, it is no vaccine at all.

## Prerequisites

- A clear immunisation register for the community and the children in it
- A cold chain with a written temperature log
- A named person trained to recognise and respond to anaphylaxis
- A referral route to a clinic for cases beyond field capability

## Materials & Tools

- Vaccine vials with batch number, expiry date, and vial monitor
- Insulated cold chain carrier with conditioned coolant packs
- A temperature monitor or minimum/maximum thermometer for the carrier
- Auto-disable syringes in the sizes the schedule requires
- Diluent matched to each vaccine that needs it
- Alcohol handrub, sterile swabs, and gloves
- A sharps container and a sealed clinical waste bag
- Adverse event forms and a batch register
- A timer and a quiet waiting area

## Procedure

### Store and Transport

1. Keep most refrigerated vaccines between +2 degrees C and +8 degrees C,
   and never freeze one, because freezing destroys several of them.
2. Condition the coolant pack until it is cold but not frozen so vials
   never sit against ice, and keep the carrier closed and shaded.
3. Record the storage temperature twice a day and at every transfer, and
   check the vaccine vial monitor at each opening.

### Plan Coverage

1. List the diseases in the national or regional schedule, and map the
   schedule onto the birth cohort and the catch-up cohort.
2. Trace the register to find the children who were missed, and schedule
   sessions on market days and school days so families can attend.
3. Book the second dose against the interval given in the schedule, and
   plan a surge session after any missed round.

### Run the Session

1. Check the expiry date, the batch number, and the cold chain log before
   the first dose of the day, and screen each person for contraindications
   using the national screening questions.
2. Reconstitute the vaccine only with the diluent named on the label, draw
   the dose with a sterile syringe, one per person, and give it by the
   route on the label into the correct site.
3. Record the batch number, the date, the site, and the name of the
   vaccinator, watch each person for 15 minutes, and put the used syringe
   straight into the sharps container.

### Respond to Adverse Events

1. Keep the person lying down and do not leave them alone.
2. Treat anaphylaxis with adrenaline only if you are trained and following
   the national protocol, and send for medical help at once.
3. Report the event to the surveillance system within 24 hours, keep the
   vial and the record so the batch can be traced, and tell the supplier
   if other cases share that batch.

## Safety Notes

- Giving the wrong product, the wrong route, or the wrong dose is the most
  common preventable harm in a session; read every label aloud.
- Use a new sterile needle and syringe for every dose; never reuse one.
- A broken cold chain makes a vaccine useless without looking wrong, so
  log the temperature every time.
- A needlestick needs immediate care; do not squeeze or scrub the wound,
  and report it the same day.
- Keep an adrenaline kit and a trained responder present at every session.
- Do not vaccinate during acute severe illness; follow national
  guidance on deferral.

## Overview

The productivity of the sea rests on a short food chain, so every catch
removes biomass that has to regrow before it can be taken again. Knowing
the trophic levels, the age structure of the catch, and the size of the
nursery grounds turns fishing from taking into managing. The key
principle: harvest only the fraction of the stock the population can
replace in a year.

## Prerequisites

- A local fish identification guide and knowledge of the food web
- A catch recording system and a scale that works in the wet
- Tide tables and a chart of the fishing grounds

## Materials & Tools

- A local fish identification guide, in waterproof form
- A measuring board or callipers reading to 1 mm
- A spring balance or scale reading to 100 g
- A cast net, seine, or hand line appropriate to the fishery
- Numbered tags and a tag applicator for marking releases
- Waterproof data sheets and a pencil
- Temperature, salinity, and pH meters
- Bait, ice, and insulated boxes for the catch
- A ruler, knife, and a sampling tray for gut and scale samples

## Procedure

### Assess the Stock

1. Sample the same grounds and the same months every year, and repeat the
   sample as close as possible to the same date each year.
2. Measure each fish to the nearest millimetre and weigh it to the nearest
   100 g, then take scale or otolith samples from a sample of the catch.
3. Build an age-length table, find the age at first maturity, record the
   proportion of large old spawners left in the catch, and compare catch
   per unit of effort between years and between grounds.

### Read the Ecosystem

1. Measure bottom temperature and salinity at each station, and note
   plankton blooms, water clarity, and the depth of the thermocline.
2. Record the seabed habitat as rock, sand, kelp, or mud, and map the
   nursery grounds, especially the seagrass and mangrove edges.
3. Record spawner aggregations, seabird concentrations, whale sightings,
   jellyfish swarms, algal blooms, and dead fish events.

### Set and Enforce Catch Limits

1. Use the age-length table to estimate the biomass that is still growing,
   and hold the annual catch below the replacement rate of the stock.
2. Close the nursery grounds, protect the spawning season of each
   species, and enforce a minimum size that matches the age at first
   maturity.
3. Use mesh large enough that undersized fish escape the gear, and record
   every landing, including discards, in the community log.

### Rebuild a Depleted Stock

1. Reduce the catch below the replacement rate for several seasons.
2. Protect the spawning aggregations and the nursery grounds, and stop the
   destructive bottom gear.
3. Watch the age-length table for a return of older, larger fish, and raise
   the catch limit only after the stock has rebuilt measurably.

## Safety Notes

- Never fish alone; carry a life jacket and a working radio or phone.
- Cold water shock and drowning kill quickly, so wear the jacket in calm
  weather too.
- Beware of rip currents when wading over reef or sand flats, and know the
  escape route before you enter.
- Use a dehooker and gloves for large fish; never handle a shark bare
  handed.
- Watch for red tide and paralytic shellfish poisoning; do not eat
  shellfish from a closed area.
- Secure the catch in a cool box on ice; spoiled fish carries a real
  health risk.

## Overview

Membranes decide what enters and leaves a cell, and the same lipid film that
keeps a cell intact drives the diffusion experiments used in classrooms and
clinics. Osmosis explains why a wilted vegetable firms up in salt water and why
infusion fluids must match the patient's blood. The key principle is that
solutes and water move down their own concentration gradients across a
selectively permeable membrane, and only an energy-driven pump can move a
solute uphill.

## Prerequisites

- Basic chemistry and the ability to make solutions by mass
- A knife and a cutting board handled safely
- A place to store samples for an hour without disturbance

## Materials & Tools

- Potatoes, carrots, or a live aquatic plant
- Table salt and sugar
- Distilled water and tap water
- Balance accurate to 0.1 g, plus a kitchen scale or graduated cylinders
- Sharp knife, cork borer, and cutting board
- Cups or small beakers with lids, and labels
- Paper towels and a ruler
- Clock or watch
- Dialysis tubing and rubber bands, if available
- Neutral red indicator, if available, for the membrane test

## Procedure

### Stage 1: Prepare the solutions

1. Make at least four concentrations of a single solute, for example 0, 0.5,
   1.0, and 2.0 molar sodium chloride, recording each as a mass of solute per
   litre, and label every cup with its concentration and the date.
2. Use distilled water for one series and tap water for another to show the
   effect of solutes already dissolved.

### Stage 2: Prepare the tissue

1. Wash the potato or carrot, then cut equal cylinders of 25 mm diameter and
   5 mm thickness with the cork borer or the knife.
2. Weigh each cylinder, rinse the starch off the cut faces, then blot it dry
   and weigh it again so that any later change is unambiguous.

### Stage 3: Run the osmosis test

1. Place the cylinders in the solutions so that each is fully submerged, and
   label the cups to match.
2. Leave them for 30 to 60 minutes, then weigh each cylinder again and record
   the change.
3. Plot the percentage mass change against the solution concentration. The
   line crosses zero at the isotonic point.
4. Keep one cylinder in distilled water as a control.

### Stage 4: Investigate the membrane itself

1. Fill a dialysis tubing sachet with a concentrated sugar solution, close
   it, and suspend it in distilled water.
2. Compare the final volumes inside the tubing and in the surrounding liquid
   to show water moving while the solute stays behind, and add a drop of
   neutral red to see whether the indicator stays inside the membrane or
   diffuses through it.

### Stage 5: Watch a living cell membrane

1. Place a piece of red onion epidermis in 5 percent salt solution and
   observe plasmolysis under the microscope at 400x.
2. Replace the salt solution with distilled water and watch the cells become
   turgid again within a few minutes.

## Safety Notes

- The main hazards at the microscope bench are the 100x objective and the heat
  of the lamp. Follow the cell biology and microscopy entry for the detailed
  rules.
- Salt solutions at 2 molar and above irritate skin and eyes. Rinse any
  splash with plenty of water.
- Do not eat any of the plant material used in the experiment, and keep the
  knives, boards, and containers away from food preparation.
- The cork borer and the knife cause cuts. Use a cutting board, cut away from
  yourself, and carry the blades pointed down.
- Wash your hands after handling soil, plant surfaces, or pond water, which
  can carry soil-transmitted pathogens.
- Use clean water for the experiment. Contaminated water gives a wrong result
  and grows organisms during the wait.
- Keep the samples labelled and out of reach of children and animals, since
  concentrated salt solution is harmful if drunk.

## Overview

Inheritance follows predictable rules, so crop and livestock traits can be
bred on purpose instead of by luck. Monohybrid and dihybrid crosses show how
alleles segregate and recombine, and repeated selection turns that knowledge
into a reliable line. The key principle: a trait only becomes a stable line
when it is selected for in every generation and the crosses are recorded.

## Prerequisites

- A basic understanding of cells, chromosomes, and gametes
- A seed tray, pots, and a well-drained growing medium
- Labels and a field notebook for recording every cross
- Isolation bags or a screen cage to keep unwanted pollen out

## Materials & Tools

- Parent seed or planting stock of both lines
- Pots, seed trays, and growing medium
- Hand lens or loupe for examining flowers
- Notebook or ledger for cross and harvest records

## Procedure

### Planning the Cross

1. Choose one trait to work on first, such as seed coat colour or plant
   height, and record the parent phenotypes you can see.
2. Confirm that each parent is homozygous by selfing it for two generations
   and checking that the offspring match the parent.
3. Decide the mating scheme: a monohybrid cross for one trait, or a
   dihybrid cross for two traits tracked at once.
4. Label every pot and seed packet before crossing so the pedigree stays
   traceable.

### Making the Cross

1. Emasculate the female flower by removing the anthers early in the
   morning, before the pollen sheds, and bag it to keep stray pollen out.
2. Collect fresh pollen from the second parent and apply it to the stigma
   the same day.
3. Rebag and label the flower with both parent names and the date.

### Reading the Offspring

1. Grow the F1 seed and score each plant. Expect a uniform generation
   showing the dominant phenotype when the parents differ.
2. Self the F1 plants to produce the F2 seed, then grow the F2 generation
   and count the phenotypes.
3. Expect roughly 3:1 for a single dominant trait, or 9:3:3:1 for two
    independent traits, and test the fit with a chi-square test.
4. Keep only the lines whose segregation fits, then select the F2 plants
    that show the desired trait and self them.

### Fixing the Trait

1. Repeat selfing and selection for four to six generations until the
    offspring are uniform, then archive seed and record the pedigree, the
    selection criteria, and the harvest year.

## Safety Notes

- Never eat, taste, or brew any plant or seed used in a trial; many crop
  relatives and their wild relatives are toxic.
- Wear gloves and wash hands after handling, since seed and plant material
  can carry fungal and viral pathogens.
- Keep trial plots away from food crops so no experimental material reaches
  a harvest.
- Work in a ventilated space so that dry seed and chaff dust are not
  inhaled.
- Keep every label legible, because one mislabelled cross wastes a season
  and corrupts the whole ledger.

## Overview

PCR turns a trace of DNA into a visible band within hours, so a field clinic
can identify pathogens, crop pests, or adulterated food without a central
laboratory. The result is only as trustworthy as the controls that ran beside
it. The key principle: keep amplified DNA out of the clean area, or the
test will read your own contamination as a positive result.

## Prerequisites

- Formal training in PCR setup and contamination control
- A separated pre-amplification area and a post-amplification area
- Access to a thermocycler and a gel electrophoresis rig
- Pure water, calibrated pipettes, and filter tips
- A working relationship with a reference laboratory

## Materials & Tools

- Specimen: swab, tissue, sputum, or a concentrated water sample
- DNA extraction kit, or a lysis and alcohol precipitation protocol
- PCR master mix with a hot-start polymerase
- Forward and reverse primers for the target organism
- Positive control DNA and a no-template control
- Thermocycler, heat block, and consumables
- Agarose, running buffer, DNA stain, and a DNA ladder
- UV or blue-light transilluminator, and a microcentrifuge

## Procedure

### Extracting the DNA

1. Pre-aliquot the reagents in the clean area before any sample is opened,
   then collect, label, and keep the specimen cool for same-day processing.
2. Lyse the specimen and remove proteins with a salt or alcohol wash, using
   the volumes given for the kit in use.
3. Transfer the DNA pellet to a clean tube with nuclease-free water, keep it
   on ice, and estimate or measure the concentration.

### Setting Up the Reaction

1. Prepare the master mix in the clean area, for all reactions plus ten
   percent extra, at the volumes the polymerase maker specifies.
2. Add template DNA last, change tips after every tube, and never pipette
   with an open amplified tube anywhere near the bench.
3. Include a positive control with known DNA and a no-template control
   filled with water, close the tubes, and spin them briefly.

### Running the Thermocycler

1. Program 25 to 35 cycles of 94 to 95 degrees C for 30 seconds, 50 to 65
   degrees C for 30 seconds, and 72 degrees C for 30 to 60 seconds per
   kilobase of product.
2. Hold at 72 degrees C for 5 minutes, then hold at 4 degrees C, and record
   the program, the run time, and the operator in the log.

### Reading the Gel

1. Cast a 1.5 to 2 percent agarose gel in running buffer, load it with a
   DNA ladder, and load 5 to 10 microlitres of each reaction with dye.
2. Run the gel at 100 to 120 volts until the dye front is about two thirds
    down the gel.
3. Visualise with a DNA stain under the transilluminator, then photograph
    and score the bands.
4. Report a sample as positive only when a band sits at the expected size
    and both controls behaved correctly.

## Safety Notes

- Ultraviolet light from the transilluminator burns skin and eyes; use a
  shield or a blue-light transilluminator and never look at the source.
- Ethidium bromide and related DNA stains are mutagenic; prefer safer
  blue-light stains, wear gloves, and treat stained gels and buffers as
  chemical waste.
- Opening an amplified tube can aerosolise product and contaminate the
  pipette tip, the bench, and every later reaction.
- Specimens may carry hepatitis, tuberculosis, or other blood-borne
  pathogens; treat every sample as infectious and wear gloves, a coat, and
  eye protection.
- Broken glass and gel-slicing tools cause deep cuts; use a gel scoop and
  put glass in puncture-proof containers.
- Work with sharp blades and forceps under a stable light, and never cut
  towards your hand.

## Overview

Photosynthesis turns light, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen,
and every crop yield depends on how well a plant manages that trade.
Understanding the light and dark reactions, the limits set by light, water,
and nutrients, and the meaning of deficiency symptoms turns a field
inspection into a diagnosis. The key principle: whichever factor is
shortest sets the pace of the whole crop.

## Prerequisites

- Plant cell and leaf anatomy basics
- A plot or pot of the crop under study, plus a comparison planting
- A soil test, or at least a pH meter

## Materials & Tools

- Healthy and stressed sample plants for side-by-side comparison
- Soil or growing medium samples and a soil test kit
- A refractometer or Brix meter for sap and juice sugar readings
- Light meter or a simple lux meter for canopy readings
- Hand lens, labels, and a notebook for each sample

## Procedure

### Mapping the Two Stages

1. Split the process into the light reactions, which run in the thylakoid
   membrane and produce ATP and NADPH, and the dark reactions, which build
   sugar in the stroma using that energy.
2. Trace the carbon: six CO2 molecules enter the cycle and leave as one
   glucose, at the cost of about 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
3. Note that photorespiration returns carbon to the cycle, and that C4
   plants concentrate CO2 near RuBisCO to cut that loss in hot climates.

### Finding the Limiting Factor

1. Measure the light level at the canopy with a meter; above roughly
   30 000 lux most crops are already at light saturation.
2. Watch the stomata: they close when water is short, and a closed stomaton
   cuts photosynthesis and transpiration together.
3. Measure water use, since a healthy crop transpires about 2 to 5 grams of
   water for every gram of dry matter produced.
4. Watch the leaf temperature; above about 30 to 35 degrees C
   photorespiration rises and photosynthesis falls.
5. Change one factor at a time, whether water, light, or nutrients, and
   record the response each time.

### Reading Nutrient Status

1. Take a soil sample from the root zone and test it, aiming for pH 6.0 to
   6.5 for most garden crops.
2. Compare leaf colour against a deficiency chart; nitrogen shortage shows
    as pale older leaves first, while iron shortage shows as pale young
    leaves with green veins.
3. Use the plant's total demand as a guide: nitrogen at 2 to 3 percent of
    dry mass, phosphorus at 0.2 to 0.5 percent, and potassium at 1 to 3
    percent.
4. Correct a confirmed deficiency with a targeted fertiliser rather than a
    general one, and record the rate applied and the date.

## Safety Notes

- Many fertilisers are harmful if swallowed; wear gloves when handling them
  and store them away from food, feed, and animals.
- Some plants carry toxic sap, latex, or alkaloids; wear gloves when
  cutting or mulching and wash your hands afterwards.
- Never apply fresh manure to edible crops close to harvest, and never burn
  manure or residues that may carry pathogens.
- Keep children, pets, and water sources out of any treated area, and
  follow the label interval on every pesticide.
- Use only mature compost, since unfinished compost carries weed seed and
  human pathogens.
- Wear eye protection when slicing stalks and when handling plants with
  irritating hairs or thorns.

## Overview

Propagation multiplies a plant exactly, and grafting combines the roots of
one plant with the top of another. Seed gives new varieties, cuttings give
copies, and grafting gives a better root system or an earlier crop. The key
principle: every graft needs live cambium touching live cambium, and every
cutting must stay moist until it has rooted.

## Prerequisites

- Plant physiology and plant cell basics
- A rooting area where humidity can be held
- A sharp knife and grafting tools in good order

## Materials & Tools

- Mother plants of the varieties to propagate
- Sharp grafting knife, secateurs, and grafting tape
- Rooting medium: perlite, coarse sand, or a 1:1 perlite and peat mix
- Seed trays, pots, and a humidity dome or clear cover
- Rooting hormone powder for hard cuttings
- Labels, a pencil, and a propagation record sheet

## Procedure

### Raising from Seed

1. Test seed viability by soaking 10 seeds in water; seeds that sink are
   usually the viable ones.
2. Break dormancy where it is needed, by holding moist seed at 1 to 5
   degrees C for 2 to 12 weeks.
3. Sow at a depth of about three times the seed width and keep the medium
   at 20 to 25 degrees C.
4. Move the seedlings into full light as soon as the first true leaves
   appear.

### Rooting from Cuttings

1. Take hardwood cuttings from dormant wood, semi-hardwood cuttings from
   partly ripened shoots, and softwood cuttings from the tips of active
   growth.
2. Cut a clean 10 to 15 cm shoot with a sharp blade just below a node, and
   strip the lower leaves.
3. Dip the base in rooting hormone and insert it two thirds deep into the
   moist medium.
4. Enclose the tray in a humidity dome and hold it at 20 to 25 degrees C out
   of direct sun.
5. Check for roots after 3 to 6 weeks by tugging a cutting gently; pot it
   up when it resists the pull.

### Grafting and Budding

1. Graft in late winter or early spring, while the stock is dormant and the
    sap has not started to move, and make a clean 3 to 5 cm cut on both the
    stock and the scion with a full face of cambium.
2. Use a whip-and-tongue graft when the diameters match, and a splice or
    bark graft when the scion is smaller, then wrap the union tightly and
    coat it with grafting wax.
3. Check the graft after 2 to 3 weeks, remove rootstock suckers as they
    appear, and cut back above the union once the graft is growing
    strongly.

## Safety Notes

- Cutting tools cause deep cuts; use a sharp blade, cut away from your
  body, and keep your fingers behind the edge.
- Sap from many plants is irritating or toxic; wear gloves and wash after
  handling cuttings.
- Bitumen-based grafting wax sticks to skin and can burn when it warms in
  sunlight; apply it in the shade and wash it off with warm soapy water.
- Keep rooting hormone powders sealed and labelled, and store them away
  from kitchen stores and food crops.
- Work in a ventilated space when using horticultural solvents or resin
  grafting tapes.
- Clean tools between plants so that viruses and bacteria are not carried
  from one stock to the next.

## Overview

Insects are the pollinators that move pollen between flowers and the
decomposers that move nutrients through soil. Building habitat for them
and protecting colonies from pesticides is one of the cheapest ways to raise
crop yield. The key principle: a farm needs forage across the whole season,
so something must be blooming in every month of it.

## Prerequisites

- A basic knowledge of insect life cycles
- A survey of the land and the vegetation already on it
- Materials for nest boxes and for a planted border

## Materials & Tools

- Bee boxes or a top-bar hive with frames
- Nesting bundles of hollow bamboo, reed stems, or drilled wood blocks
- Bare ground and mud for solitary ground-nesting bees
- Flower seed for a mixed border with early and late bloomers
- A water source with shallow landing stones
- Insect hotels of stacked wood blocks, pipe, and cardboard tubes
- Protective gear: veil, gloves, smoker, and a hive tool
- Record sheets for colony counts and garden pollinator counts

## Procedure

### Understanding the Life Cycle

1. Map the stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult for complete metamorphosis,
   or egg and nymph for incomplete metamorphosis.
2. Note the scale of a colony: 60 000 honey bee workers make about 2
   million foraging trips a day, each visit to a single flower.
3. Watch the brood cycle of about 21 days from egg to emerging adult in the
   honey bee, and time the work to the local foraging calendar rather than
   to the calendar month.

### Providing Habitat

1. Provide the three resources in balance: about 40 percent bare ground
   for ground-nesting bees, 30 percent hollow cavities, and 30 percent
   hollow stems.
2. Site hives in a sheltered spot with morning sun, out of the prevailing
   wind, with water within a few hundred metres.
3. Add brood boxes in steps; a colony needs roughly 0.5 to 1 cubic metre
   of space as it grows through the season.
4. Fill nesting bundles with hollow stems of 5 to 10 mm diameter and clear
   them each spring, and drill holes 5 to 8 mm across and 10 cm deep into
   a block of untreated wood for solitary bees.
5. Plant a mixed border that gives at least three species in bloom in
   every month, with both a nectar source and a pollen source.

### Protecting the Colony

1. Inspect for varroa mites, and requeen a colony that shows a spotty brood
   pattern.
2. Plan for the swarm season: a colony may leave with 5 to 10 kg of bees
    and half its strength.
3. Do not spray insecticides while crops are blooming, and if spraying is
    unavoidable, treat at night and leave an unsprayed refuge of at least a
    third of the land.
4. Prefer insecticidal soaps and oils over broad-spectrum insecticides,
    keep them out of the bloom, reduce mowing and tillage, leave
    uncultivated strips through the winter, and keep a year-on-year count
    of colonies and pollinator visits so the trend stays visible.

## Safety Notes

- Stings cause allergic reactions and anaphylaxis in a small number of
  people; keep hives at least 25 metres from public paths and wear a veil
  and gloves.
- Never open a honey bee colony without protective clothing, a clear exit
  to the rear, and a smoker, since stings become more likely in bad
  weather.
- Many insects carry disease; never handle stinging insects bare-handed,
  and never apply an insecticide without reading the label and wearing the
  protection it names.
- Insecticides are toxic to people, pets, and aquatic life; lock them
  away, never decant them into drink bottles, and respect the harvest
  interval on the label.
- Old nests, bee debris, and rotten wood carry fungal spores and mites;
  wear a mask when disturbing old insect habitat.
- Check local rules and the landowner's permission before moving hives or
  collecting wild nests.

## Overview

Soil is a living system in which bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and worms turn
dead matter into plant nutrients. Composting is that process under control,
and getting the carbon to nitrogen ratio, the moisture, and the temperature
right turns waste into a soil amendment. The key principle: compost is
finished when the pile stops heating and no longer smells of ammonia.

## Prerequisites

- A basic understanding of plant nutrients and soil texture
- Space for a pile, with water and a fork or turner to hand
- A thermometer long enough to reach the centre of the pile

## Materials & Tools

- Dry brown material: straw, shredded cardboard, dry leaves, small twigs
- Green material: grass clippings, vegetable scraps without meat, manure
- Water and a hose or watering can
- A pile thermometer, a pitchfork, and a tarp
- Screening wire and a bucket for the finished compost

## Procedure

### Building the Pile

1. Choose a shaded, well-drained site and build a heap roughly 1 m by 1 m
   by 1.5 m for a small batch.
2. Lay a base of coarse sticks 10 cm deep so that air can move beneath the
   pile.
3. Alternate 15 cm layers of brown and green material, and mix in a
   handful of finished compost as the starter.
4. Aim for a carbon to nitrogen ratio of about 25 to 30 parts carbon to one
   part nitrogen; greens alone run near 10 to 15 and browns near 50 to 100.
5. Water each layer until the material feels like a wrung-out sponge, at
   roughly 40 to 60 percent moisture.

### Managing the Pile

1. Check the centre temperature daily; a healthy pile reaches 55 to 65
   degrees C within a week.
2. Hold the pile in that range for at least 3 days, or turn it 5 times and
   hold it for 15 days, so the heat kills most weed seeds and pathogens.
3. Turn the pile when it cools, or when the centre stays more than 10
   degrees C above the edges, which shows the edges are too dry.
4. Re-wet dry patches, and add more brown material if the pile smells of
   ammonia or turns sour.

### Testing and Harvesting

1. Expect a fast pile to finish in 6 to 8 weeks and a slow one in 3 to 6
    months; check that the pile no longer heats after turning and smells of
    earth rather than ammonia.
2. Squeeze a handful: it should hold together and then break apart when
    pressed, not form a dense ball.
3. Sieve the compost to 10 to 15 mm, test it in a seed tray with radish or
    lettuce for normal germination in 4 to 7 days, and store the finished
    compost under cover for up to a year.

## Safety Notes

- A working pile reaches 65 degrees C and will burn skin; probe it with a
  long thermometer and never put your hand into the centre.
- Decomposing material can produce carbon monoxide in a sealed space, so
  keep the pile outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed.
- Animal manure and kitchen scraps can carry pathogens such as E. coli and
  Salmonella; do not use this compost on edible crops close to harvest.
- Dry compost dust irritates the lungs; wear a mask when sieving or
  handling a dusty pile.
- Honey bees and other insects swarm warm compost; do not site the pile near
  an apiary.
- Keep the pile away from wells and watercourses so that nutrient-rich
  runoff cannot reach streams.
