## Overview

Computer vision turns a grid of numbers into a statement about the world.
The pipeline always has the same shape: fix the image, find features, feed
a classifier, then check the result against reality. The key principle is
that the pixels are only the input: the work that matters is in the
training set and in an honest measurement of what the system gets wrong,
because a vision model scored only on easy examples fails on the first
hard night.

## Prerequisites

- Linear algebra basics: vectors, matrices, and dot products
- Basic statistics and the idea of a distribution
- Python with an array library and an imaging library
- Machine Learning Fundamentals

## Materials & Tools

- Camera with a known resolution and lens, or a fixed image dataset
- Image library able to read and write the common formats
- Scripting environment for batch processing and plotting
- Labelled image set with a written labelling guide
- Plotting tool for histograms, confusion matrices, and precision-recall
  curves
- Storage for the raw images and a manifest of every file
- Annotation tool, and a second person to check a sample of the labels

## Procedure

### Prepare the images

1. Record the resolution, the colour depth, and the format of every
   source, and check for colour and orientation errors before use.
2. Convert to a consistent form, either 8-bit grayscale with 256 levels
   for shape work or 8 bits per colour channel for colour work, and write
   a manifest of the conversion.
3. Normalise brightness and contrast against a fixed reference, and leave
   the original files untouched.

### Extract features

1. Apply a Gaussian blur with a radius of about 1 percent of the image
   width to suppress noise before any edge or shape work.
2. Find edges with a gradient operator such as Sobel, whose weighting of
   1, 2, 1 along each axis makes it less sensitive to noise than a plain
   difference.
3. Segment the image into regions and describe each region by simple
   measurements: area, aspect ratio, mean colour, and edge orientation.

### Train a classifier

1. Split the labelled images into about 60 percent for training, 20
   percent for validation, and 20 percent for the sealed test, and keep
   the split fixed.
2. Train a simple classifier, such as a support vector machine or a
   nearest-neighbour model, and tune it on the validation set only.
3. Score the result on the sealed test set with the confusion matrix, and
   report precision and recall per class rather than one overall number.

### Deploy with checks

1. Extend the training set with augmentation that matches the real
   variations: brightness, scale, rotation, blur, and partial occlusion.
2. Run the classifier on a live feed or a fresh sample and compare the
   output with a human reading the same images.
3. Log the inputs, the outputs, and the failures, and set a schedule for
   reviewing the results and retraining when the conditions change.

## Safety Notes

- A camera pointed at people captures them. Get consent, post a notice,
  and restrict access to the recordings as you would any private record.
- Never let a vision system control machinery without an independent
  interlock and a human override that works when the system is wrong.
- Do not build a system that identifies or tracks individuals for
  surveillance without an agreed governance and a stated purpose.
- Check the eye-safety class of any infrared illuminator or laser
  rangefinder before mounting it where people or animals can look into it.
- Outdoor cameras need weatherproof housings, drip loops on every cable,
  and surge protection on any line that leaves the building.
- Under-represented groups are misidentified more often, so measure the
  error rate per group and per lighting condition before trusting the
  system.
- A model trained on one season or one camera position will fail when
  either changes; keep the mount rigid and re-check the results after any
  disturbance.

## Overview

Cryptography is the part of computing where a small mistake stays hidden
until it matters. A cipher that works on the test data can still be
unsafe because the nonce repeated, the key came from a password, or the
comparison was not constant time. The key principle is that the algorithm
is the easy part: correct use of a standard primitive with sound key
handling is worth far more than a clever scheme of your own.

## Prerequisites

- Embedded C Programming, or equivalent fluency in C
- Modular arithmetic and the idea of a one-way function
- Basic networking, so you know where a key travels
- Record keeping disciplined enough to never improvise a primitive

## Materials & Tools

- An audited cryptographic library with documented primitives
- A cryptographically secure random source with a self test
- A hardware token or key store, if the platform provides one
- Password hashing tool with a tunable cost parameter
- Reference test vectors from the standard for each primitive in use
- Two machines for a key exchange test, and a packet capture for review
- A ledger of key identifiers, rotation dates, and owners

## Procedure

### Classify the data

1. Decide what each piece of data is: public, needing confidentiality,
   needing integrity only, or needing a verifiable signature.
2. Map each requirement onto one primitive and write the choice down
   before any code is written.
3. Set the key lifetime and the rotation interval from the risk and the
   cost of re-keying.

### Manage the keys

1. Generate every key with the system's secure random source, never with
   a general purpose random number generator.
2. Derive keys from passwords with a memory-hard function such as
   Argon2id, or with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at a cost of at least 600000
   iterations, and give every password a random salt of at least 16 bytes.
3. Keep long-term keys away from the code and from the backups they
   protect, and wrap them with a key held in a passphrase or a token.

### Encrypt and authenticate

1. Use an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, and
   generate a fresh random nonce of 12 bytes for every message under a
   given key.
2. Bind the context into the authenticated data, so a message cannot be
   moved from one context to another without being detected.
3. Compare the tags in constant time and reject any message that fails,
   before acting on any part of the plaintext.

### Verify and maintain

1. Run the reference test vectors from the standard for every primitive
   and record the results.
2. Test the failure paths: a wrong key, a truncated message, a repeated
   nonce, and an expired certificate must all be rejected.
3. Rotate the keys on schedule, revoke what must be revoked, and keep an
   audit trail of every use.

## Safety Notes

- The hazard here is false security. A misused or weak cipher gives the
  same confidence as a strong one while protecting nothing, so use
  libraries and primitives reviewed by others and never invent one.
- Only do this work with appropriate training, supervision, and
  equipment, and have designs that handle authentication or personal data
  reviewed by qualified people.
- Keys hard-coded in source, firmware, or an image can be extracted from
  the device, so treat any key in a binary as public.
- Keys stored on the same medium as the data they protect protect
  nothing against theft of that medium.
- Randomness from a weak source makes every derived key guessable, and
  the failure is silent.
- Constant-time comparison matters: a byte-by-byte early exit leaks the
  correct value one byte at a time.
- Passwords must not be stored reversibly, must not be logged, and must
  not use a fast hash such as MD5 or SHA-256 without a work factor.
- Never disable certificate or host verification to make a connection
  succeed; that is exactly how a connection gets intercepted.
- Keep key material out of logs, crash dumps, swap, and backups unless
  those stores are protected as carefully as the keys themselves.

## Overview

Storage is a ladder of trade-offs between speed, capacity, and how long a
record survives. A filesystem turns a block device into named files with
permissions, and above it a backup and an archive keep the data when the
machine dies. The key principle is that a copy is not a backup until it
has been read back, so the measure of a storage system is not how much it
holds but how much of it can be restored.

## Prerequisites

- Command line use and a text editor
- Basic file and directory concepts
- An understanding of what a checksum function does
- A spare disk or a virtual disk image to experiment on

## Materials & Tools

- Several disks of different sizes, or virtual disk images
- Checksum tool, archive tool, and a backup utility
- A filesystem that logs writes, such as an ext4 or btrfs volume
- A second, separate machine or network target for the off-site copy
- Antistatic kit, drive caddy, and a label maker for the disks
- A written ledger listing each disk, its contents, and its checksum
- Test files of known size to measure real throughput

## Procedure

### Choose and prepare the medium

1. Test every disk before trusting it by writing and reading back a file
   across the whole surface, then record the result on the label.
2. Choose a filesystem and mount options that suit the role, and turn on
   journalling or a checksummed mode where the medium allows it.
3. Write the partition table and the filesystem, then confirm that the
   sizes reported match the sizes on the label.

### Lay out the data

1. Follow the filesystem hierarchy for the system directories: /etc for
   configuration, /var for variable data, /home for user files, and /usr
   for read-only programs.
2. Separate the data that changes often from the data that never changes,
   so caches and backups can be handled on different schedules.
3. Record a checksum for every file and store the list with the data, so a
   later read can prove the bytes are still the ones you stored.

### Copy and verify

1. Take a full copy first, then schedule the increments, and keep the
   copies on different media from the original.
2. Follow the rule of three copies on two kinds of media, with one copy
   held somewhere else.
3. After each copy, read it back and compare the checksums, then record
   the result and the date in the ledger.

### Archive for the long term

1. Choose a format that can be read without the tool that wrote it, and
   prefer plain uncompressed files when the content matters most.
2. Fix the permissions and ownership inside the archive so it restores
   onto a new machine without guesswork.
3. Test a full restore into a clean directory, compare it with the
   original using checksums, and repeat the test on a schedule.

## Safety Notes

- A partition table written to the wrong disk destroys data without
  warning. Back up first, work on a spare disk to learn the procedure,
  and label every drive with its identifier.
- A redundant array is not a backup. A failed controller, a deleted file,
  or malware takes every copy with it, so keep one copy offline.
- The write cache in a drive lies about durability unless it is flushed.
  Enable the flush of the write cache, and back up after any unclean
  shutdown.
- Drives are fragile: never move a spinning disk while it runs, use the
  antistatic kit, and keep the drives separated and ventilated.
- Never use the only copy as the source of a destructive operation, and
  never format a device by its partition number without checking the
  serial number in the system log.
- Assume silent corruption in stored media and check the fixity of the
  archive on a schedule, not once at the start.
- Keep free space on every volume; a full filesystem can corrupt a
  database and can stop an archive from being written at all.

A calculator

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

DC circuit analysis is the discipline of turning a drawing into numbers
you can check. The key principle is that every network obeys two
conservation laws, conservation of charge and conservation of energy,
and that every method, from a simple series divider to node analysis,
is only bookkeeping for those two statements. Solve the network twice
by two different methods; if the answers disagree then one of them is
wrong, and the disagreement is the cheapest fault-finding tool there
is.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Paper, a pencil, and an eraser for the working
- A calculator
- A bench supply, 0 to 30 V, with a current limit
- A digital multimeter with a continuity and a diode function
- Resistors in the E12 series, 0.25 W, and a few capacitors and coils
- A solderless breadboard, jumper wires, and a battery for the test
  circuits

## Procedure

### Set up the network

1. Draw the circuit, label every node, mark the reference node as
   ground with a 0 V label, mark the direction of every current and the
   polarity of every source, and write the value of every component
   next to its symbol.
2. Reduce the network step by step: combine the resistors in series
   into one and the resistors in parallel into one, before writing any
   equation.

### Apply Ohm's law

1. Compute the total resistance of a series chain by adding the
   resistances, and check that the result is larger than the largest
   single resistor.
2. Compute an equivalent parallel resistance from 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 +
   the rest, and check that it is smaller than the smallest single
   resistor.
3. Use the voltage divider V_out = V_in x R2 / (R1 + R2) for a series
   pair, and the current divider I = I_total x R_other / (R1 + R2) for a
   parallel pair.

### Apply Kirchhoff's laws

1. Sum the currents entering a node and set the sum to zero, using a
   sign convention and writing the direction of each current beside the
   equation.
2. Sum the voltage changes around any closed loop and set the sum to
   zero, remembering that a rise is positive and a drop is negative.
3. Solve the simultaneous equations, then check the answer against the
   source: the power leaving the source must equal the power in the
   resistors, with P = V x I = I^2 x R = V^2 / R.

### Find the equivalent source

1. Remove the load and measure the open-circuit voltage for the
   Thevenin voltage, then short the independent voltage sources, open
   the independent current sources, and measure the resistance across
   the terminals for the Thevenin resistance.
2. Convert to the Norton form with I_N = V_th / R_th and the same
   resistance, then load the equivalent source with the real load and
   check that the current and the voltage match.

### Verify by superposition and measurement

1. Solve the network again with one source at a time and the others
   set to zero, then add the results; the total must match the first
   answer.
2. Build the circuit on the breadboard, apply the supply with the
   current limit set low, and measure the node voltages against the
   calculation; check that no resistor is dissipating more than its
   rating, because a 0.25 W resistor at full rating can reach 100 °C
   and is a fire hazard.

## Safety Notes

- Keep the work at low voltage and low current. Mains voltage is
  lethal, and 230 V across the body can stop the heart.
- A short circuit across a battery or a large supply can produce
  thousands of amps: set the current limit, fit a fuse of the right
  rating, and keep a hand on the switch.
- Charge every capacitor through a resistor before handling it, and
  discharge the large ones with a proper discharge tool rather than a
  screwdriver.
- Resistances get hot when the power is wrong; keep within the rating
  and leave a gap between the parts so that the heat can get away.
- Protect the work from static discharge: use a grounded wrist strap
  and a grounded mat for the components that cannot tolerate a shock.
- Check the polarity of every electrolytic capacitor and every diode
  before energising the circuit; reverse polarity destroys parts and
  can start a fire.

## Overview

Electronic design automation turns an idea into files a factory, a machine
shop, or a solder bench can act on without re-drawing anything. The key
principle is that the schematic is the single source of truth and everything
else, the netlist, the board layout, the drill files, and the bill of
materials, is derived from it. Keeping that whole chain inside one
versioned toolchain is what makes a design reproducible months later.

## Prerequisites

- Reading a circuit diagram and understanding schematic symbols
- The difference between a netlist, a footprint, and a drill file
- Version control basics, including commits and branching
- The difference between a component datasheet and a catalogue listing

## Materials & Tools

- KiCad 9 or later, with its symbol, footprint, and 3D model libraries
- A text editor and a spreadsheet for the bill of materials
- A PCB fabricator, or a local etching and drilling setup
- The fabricator's design rules: minimum trace width, spacing, and vias
- A multimeter, and an oscilloscope for designs with fast edges

## Procedure

### Set up the project

1. Create one project folder per board and commit it before the first board
   file exists.
2. Build a symbol library that carries the fields the fabricator needs:
   manufacturer part number, value, footprint reference, and tolerance.
3. Write a design-rules note in the project folder listing the fabricator's
   minimum trace width, spacing, and via limits, and fix the sheet size,
   the grid, and the units so every sheet is identical.

### Capture the schematic

1. Draw one sheet per functional block and use hierarchical sheets so a
   block can be reused without being redrawn.
2. Place every power rail and every ground symbol explicitly, then run the
   electrical rules checker and treat every warning as a defect until it
   has been explained.
3. Assign a footprint to every symbol, check each one against the real
   datasheet, then annotate the schematic and confirm that the reference
   designators are unique.

### Lay out the board

1. Place the connectors and the mounting holes first and fix them; the
   mechanical outline drives everything after that.
2. Pour the ground plane on an outer layer and keep it unbroken wherever
   the design allows.
3. Route the clock, the differential pairs, and the analogue inputs first,
   then the rest, and keep the analogue section away from the switching
   nodes.
4. Place the decoupling capacitors at the supply pins, run the design
   rules check with the fabricator's ruleset, and inspect the 3D view for
   parts that clash with the enclosure.

### Release the outputs

1. Generate the drill, pick-and-place, and fabrication outputs and the
   bill of materials from the same saved project, then compare the
   assembly drawing against the board file line by line.
2. Record the release in the changelog with the commit hash, the date, and
   the fabricator's part numbers, and file the released archives read-only
   beside the source.

## Safety Notes

- The CAD file is not the only artifact that matters: check every
  footprint against the datasheet, because a reversed or mis-pinned part
  fails on the board and not in the software.
- Etching and drilling a board uses acids and creates toxic waste; do that
  work only with appropriate training, supervision, and equipment.
- A soldering iron and a hot air station burn skin and start fires; use
  fume extraction and keep the tools in their stands.
- Mains-powered equipment beside a wet bench is a shock hazard; keep the
  power off and the bench dry.
- Never let a tool silently rewrite a released design; work on a branch
  and review the diff before merging.
- A board revision that is not recorded in the changelog will be built
  twice, and the second one will differ.

## Overview

Embedded C is C written for a microcontroller with no operating system
underneath it. The programmer owns the memory map, the reset vector, and
the timing of every peripheral, so source that behaves on a desktop can
be wrong on bare metal. The key principle is that the datasheet, not the
tutorial, is the specification: every register access is a write to a
fixed address, and every delay depends on a clock the programmer set.

## Prerequisites

- C programming: pointers, structures, bitwise operators, and the
  preprocessor
- Digital logic and the ability to read a timing diagram
- DC Circuit Analysis
- Basic soldering and the use of a serial terminal program

## Materials & Tools

- A Cortex-M board, for example an STM32F103 or an RP2040, on headers
- ARM GCC cross compiler, GNU Make, and a linker script for the target
- ST-Link, CMSIS-DAP, or an equivalent debug probe
- USB serial adapter with 3.3 V logic levels, and a terminal program
- Oscilloscope or logic analyser with 3 or more channels
- The target's reference manual, datasheet, and errata sheet
- Breadboard, jumper wires, LEDs, a push button, and 330 ohm resistors
- Multimeter for checking the supply rails

## Procedure

### Set up the toolchain

1. Install the ARM GCC cross compiler and confirm that it targets the
   arm-none-eabi triple with the compiler version flag.
2. Write a linker script that places the vector table at the base of flash
   and the stack at the top of SRAM, then check the section sizes after
   every build with the size utility.
3. Compile a minimal program that drives one GPIO pin and blinks an LED
   at 1 Hz, and confirm the reset behaviour of the board.

### Map the registers

1. Read the memory map in the reference manual and write down the base
   address and the bit positions of every register you intend to use.
2. Declare the peripheral structures as volatile pointers in a header file
   so that the compiler cannot cache a register value in a CPU register.
3. Enable the peripheral clock in the reset and clock control block, then
   confirm the clock is running by measuring a pin with a scope.

### Use interrupts and timers

1. Configure a 1 kHz tick from the system timer using the 24-bit reload
   value from the reference manual, and allow for the count starting at 0.
2. Write the interrupt service routine with the standard name and the
   attribute that tells the compiler to keep its stack frame small.
3. Enable the interrupt in the nested vector interrupt controller, clear
   the pending bit, and prove the timing by toggling a pin and measuring
   the period on the scope.

### Drive a peripheral and debug

1. Bring up the UART at 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, and 1 stop
   bit, and confirm several hundred bytes arrive intact.
2. Keep the linker map file with every build so you can see which section
   grew after a change and how much flash and RAM are left.
3. Attach the debugger, set a breakpoint in the handler, and read the
   stack frame and the peripheral registers to confirm the state.

## Safety Notes

- A soldering iron tip resting on a board will destroy the chip or the
  USB interface; work on an anti-static mat and set the iron temperature
  for the joint, not the board.
- Fit current limiting resistors of 330 to 1000 ohm on every LED and on
  any pin that drives an indicator, so a firmware fault cannot weld a
  driver or burn a trace.
- Lithium cells in a battery-powered board can vent and start a fire if
  they are shorted or overcharged; use a protected cell and never leave a
  charging board unattended.
- Firmware bugs act on real outputs the moment they are flashed. Test new
  firmware on the bench with the actuators disconnected, and keep a
  documented recovery path such as a bootloader or a hardware reset.
- Observe the electrostatic discharge precautions for the microcontroller,
  the probe, and any USB adapter, and ground yourself before handling.
- Keep low-voltage logic wiring away from mains wiring, and never rely on
  a firmware watchdog alone to make a system safe.

## Overview

Machine learning fits a model to data instead of writing the rule by hand.
The hard part is not the fitting, it is the honesty of the evaluation: a
model that has seen the test set during training reports a score it will
never reach in the field. The key principle is that the way the data is
split decides what the final number means, so a baseline, a held-out
set, and a written record of how the data was collected matter more than
the choice of model.

## Prerequisites

- Basic statistics: mean, variance, and correlation
- Probability and the idea of a distribution
- Python or an equivalent language with arrays and plotting
- Reading a table of numbers without being misled by it

## Materials & Tools

- A machine with a scripting environment and a notebook or spreadsheet
- A dataset with a clear question attached, of a few hundred rows or more
- The reference implementation of the model, taken from its documentation
- A plotting tool for the learning curve and the confusion matrix
- A data dictionary and an experiment log kept with the dataset
- Held-out data collected later, if the task is predictive
- A written statement of what the model will be used for and by whom

## Procedure

### Frame the problem

1. Write down the decision the model will support, and the cost of a
   false positive and of a false negative in that setting.
2. Define the target label precisely, so that two people would label the
   same case the same way.
3. Collect the data by the same process the model will meet in use, and
   record the collection conditions with it.

### Prepare the data

1. Look for missing values, duplicates, and impossible values, and decide
   case by case whether to drop, impute, or keep each one.
2. Split the data before any fitting, into about 60 percent for training,
   20 percent for validation, and 20 percent for the final test.
3. Keep the test set sealed until the end, and save the splits so the
   same experiment can be repeated exactly.

### Train and compare

1. Fit a trivial baseline first, such as always predicting the most
   common class, and record its score as the number to beat.
2. Fit a simple model, then a more complex one, changing one thing at a
   time and writing every run into the log.
3. Compare the models on the validation set with the metric you chose,
   and read the learning curve for signs of overfitting.

### Evaluate honestly

1. Evaluate the chosen model once on the sealed test set and report that
   number, not the best one from the search.
2. Break the results down by subgroup and by time period, because an
   average hides the failures.
3. State the limits of the data in the write-up, including where the
   model must not be used, and set a review date.

## Safety Notes

- A model is a tool that carries the bias of its data. Where a wrong
  answer matters, keep a trained person in the loop and record who
  reviewed each decision.
- Do not let a model make decisions about medical treatment, legal
  status, or safety without the appropriate expert involvement, and do
  not rely on any note here as medical or legal advice.
- Collect the least personal data that will do, get consent, and delete
  what is no longer needed; training data outlives the project.
- Do not deploy a model that has only been tested on data from a
  different population than the one it will serve.
- Watch for drift after deployment: the world moves on, the model does
  not, and a silent degradation is the usual failure.
- A surveillance or monitoring system built from these methods affects
  real people's lives, so agree the governance before you collect.
- Keep the data and the model versioned, and keep the ability to roll
  back to the previous version.

## Overview

Networking is a stack of layers, each adding a service on the one below:
addresses and routing, reliable delivery, names, and the application
conversation on top. Knowing which layer owns a fault makes diagnosis
mechanical instead of guesswork, because each layer has its own packets,
its own state machine, and its own tools. The key principle is that the
layers only promise what is theirs: an internet packet arrives or it does
not, and nothing above may assume delivery, order, or timing.

## Prerequisites

- DC Circuit Analysis, for the signal-level view of a link
- Basic networking vocabulary: address, port, protocol, and subnet
- Command line use and a text editor
- Reading a packet capture

## Materials & Tools

- Two or more machines on a shared switch, plus a spare machine as a peer
- Packet capture tool, protocol analyser, and a terminal program
- Cable tester and a loopback plug for the physical layer
- Router or soft router for the gateway and the routing tests
- A nameserver for the name lookups and a DHCP server on the test segment
- A configuration sheet and a written record of every change made

## Procedure

### Map the stack

1. Draw the seven layers of the model and write down the protocol, the
   address, and the port that belong to each layer you will meet.
2. Capture one request and identify the frames, packets, and segments
   inside it, naming the protocol used at each layer.
3. Note the address in each header: the media address, the internet
   address, and the transport port.

### Move packets

1. Give each test host an address and a prefix length, then confirm
   reachability with an address and route lookup.
2. Read the routing table on the router, add a static route for a test
   network, and trace the path to it.
3. Measure the round trip time and the loss to a neighbouring host, then
   repeat with the largest packet that passes without fragmenting.

### Connect and transfer

1. Open a reliable connection and watch the three-way handshake and the
   four-way close in the capture.
2. Transfer a file and compare the throughput with the bandwidth-delay
   product, checking the congestion window and the receive buffer.
3. Break the link during the transfer, watch both ends recover, and check
   the timeout and the connection state afterwards.

### Name and configure

1. Resolve a name to an address and read the answer, then look up the
   address for a name and compare the two records.
2. Watch the four-step lease exchange on the test segment and check the
   address, mask, gateway, and lease time the client received.
3. Confirm that a host with no working nameserver can still reach an
   address directly, and record the difference in the logs.

## Safety Notes

- Keep test networks isolated from any link that reaches the public
  internet. An exposed lab host is a liability for everyone behind it.
- A wrong subnet mask, a wrong default route, or a mistaken firewall rule
  can cut the whole site off the network at once. Keep console access to
  the router and write down the previous setting before changing it.
- Never operate an open resolver or a public domain name server on a small
  site; it will be used to amplify attacks against other people.
- A rogue DHCP server on the segment can hand out a false gateway and
  capture traffic. Only run DHCP on a network you control.
- Credentials sent over a plaintext protocol are readable by anyone on
  the path. Use an encrypted transport for logins and administration.
- Power over network cabling puts 48 volts DC on the pairs. Check the
  power budget before connecting a device, and never patch a live line
  into unknown equipment.
- Lines that leave the building need surge and lightning protection; a
  surge on a copper drop destroys the equipment at both ends.

## Overview

An operating system is the layer that turns hardware into a place where
programs run without stepping on one another. It owns the processor time,
the memory map, and the files, and it exposes those through system calls
and a filesystem namespace. The key principle is that the kernel enforces
the boundaries: a process may only touch the memory and the files the
kernel grants it, and everything above the kernel, including the shell,
the compiler, and the database, assumes that enforcement is real.

## Prerequisites

- Embedded C Programming
- Computer architecture and the memory hierarchy
- C with pointers and file handling
- Command line use and a text editor

## Materials & Tools

- A machine running Linux, plus a second machine to act as a peer
- Kernel documentation or source matching the running kernel version
- Build tools: compiler, linker, and make
- Shell, core utilities, and a terminal multiplexer
- System call tracer, process inspector, and packet sniffer
- A spare disk or a virtual disk image for filesystem experiments
- A load generator and a small scripting harness

## Procedure

### Follow a process

1. Start a program and inspect its identifier, its parent, its state, and
   its open file descriptors in the process table.
2. Trace its life from the fork and exec through to exit, and note which
   system calls the kernel handled on its behalf.
3. Measure the cost of a context switch and of creating a process, and
   compare both with the same work done inside one process.

### Schedule and synchronise

1. Start several processes competing for the processor and watch the run
   queue and the scheduling policy the kernel reports for them.
2. Change the priority of one process, confirm the scheduler responds,
   then restore the original priority.
3. Reproduce a race with two threads sharing a counter, fix it with a
   mutex, and confirm the count is exact over many runs.

### Manage memory

1. Inspect the address space of a running process and locate its code,
   data, heap, stack, and shared mappings.
2. Set a memory limit on a test process and watch it fail in a controlled
   way, then read the error the kernel returns.
3. Copy a large file and measure the effect of the page cache and of the
   read and write buffer sizes on throughput.

### Use the filesystem

1. Create a directory tree, list the inodes and file types, and compare
   the on-disk layout with the logical tree.
2. Fill a small filesystem until it reports an error, then check which
   operations still succeed and which fail cleanly.
3. Copy a tree with a checksum tool, corrupt one byte in the copy, and
   confirm that verification reports the damaged file.

## Safety Notes

- Run unfamiliar code as an ordinary user, never as the superuser, and
  never on the only machine that holds a copy of the data.
- Destructive commands such as removing a directory recursively do not
  check what they are pointed at. Dry-run the command, read the path
  twice, and never run it on a mounted network filesystem by accident.
- Killing a process that owns a database can leave the data inconsistent.
  Stop services in an orderly way so they can close and flush their files.
- A filesystem that fills up corrupts databases before it reports the
  error. Keep a margin of free space and monitor it.
- Understand the mount options before mounting anything: a sync, noexec,
  or nosuid setting changes what the filesystem will allow.
- Permissions and ownership mistakes expose private files. Review the
  group and mode of new shared directories and files.
- Back up before experimenting with partitions, and remember that a
  filesystem can lose the last writes if the machine is powered off
  without a flush.

## Overview

A printed circuit board is a mechanical drawing, a wiring diagram, and a
stack of dielectric layers, and it works only when all three agree. The
key principle is that the layout is constrained by manufacturing, so
every rule broken in the editor comes back as a board that is
expensive, slow, or rejected. Define the stack-up, respect the design
rules of the fabricator, keep the ground plane continuous, and check
the outputs against the drawing before the panels are cut.

## Prerequisites

- Schematic capture and the ability to read a netlist
- The pin data of every component in the library
- An understanding of the layers of a board, and of the surface and
  through-hole technologies
- The design rules of the fabricator, expressed in the units of the
  design tool
- The ability to read a Gerber file and an Excellon drill file

## Materials & Tools

- A schematic and layout editor with a metric and an imperial grid
- A component library with the footprints from the manufacturer
  datasheets
- The IPC-2221 design rules and the IPC-2152 current-carrying tables
- FR-4 laminate with a glass transition temperature of at least 130 °C
  and a UL94 V-0 rating
- Copper thickness of 35 µm for 1 oz or 70 µm for 2 oz
- A Gerber exporter, an Excellon drill exporter, and a CAM viewer
- A stencilled assembly drawing and a bill of materials
- A continuity and insulation test set, and a bench supply with a
  current limit for the first power-up

## Procedure

### Capture the schematic

1. Draw the schematic with correct pin numbers and names, check every
   symbol against the datasheet rather than against another drawing,
   then run the electrical rules check and resolve every unconnected
   pin, every missing power flag, and every net that has only one
   connection.
2. Produce the netlist and freeze it against a revision number before
   any layout work starts.

### Set the stack-up and the rules

1. Choose the layer count and the construction: for a four-layer board,
   a signal layer, a solid ground plane, a power plane, and a second
   signal layer, with a total thickness of 1.6 mm.
2. Load the design rules for the fabricator and the board house, a
   minimum track of 0.25 mm and a minimum gap of 0.2 mm for outer
   copper on 1.6 mm FR-4 with 1 oz copper, set the net classes, and use
   the current capacity table to widen every track that carries more
   than about 2 A.

### Lay out the board

1. Place the connectors and the mounting holes first, on the board
   outline, and keep the fixings clear of the copper.
2. Place the decoupling capacitors at the supply pins, within 5 mm of
   the pin they serve, then route the signals so that the ground plane
   stays unbroken and the return path under the signal has no split.
3. Add the silkscreen, the polarity marks, the pin numbers, and the
   board reference, then run the design rule check and confirm that
   the copper stays 0.5 mm inside the routed edge.

### Prepare the fabrication outputs

1. Export the Gerber files for the copper, the solder mask, the
   silkscreen, and the outline, and the Excellon drill file, and name
   the files with the revision.
2. Read the Gerber and the drill files back into the CAM viewer and
   layer them against each other, checking that the drill hits the
   pad, that the mask opens the pad, and that the outline matches the
   drawing.
3. Write the fabrication drawing with the stack-up, the copper weight,
   the surface finish, the solder mask colour, the tolerances, the
   electrical test requirement, and the impedance requirement if the
   board has controlled-impedance nets, then send the outputs to the
   fabricator and ask for the manufacturability report before the
   panels are cut.

### Assemble and test

1. Bake the boards if the assembly process needs it, apply the solder
   paste through a stencil or hand-solder the through-hole parts with
   the technique in the soldering entry, and reflow the board at the
   profile the paste requires: a lead-free paste with a peak near
   245 °C and a soak of 60 to 90 seconds above 150 °C.
2. Inspect the joints, power the board up for the first time from a
   current-limited supply with the limit set to about 200 mA while you
   watch the current, and check the rails against the design; if the
   current limit trips, find the short before applying power again.

## Safety Notes

- Etching and the fabrication chemistry are the hazard: the etchant,
  the stripper, and the developer are corrosive and some are toxic.
  Work with eye protection, gloves, and a chemical assessment, and
  dispose of the waste through a proper route.
- Soldering on the board releases flux fumes and, on a leaded process,
  lead; use the fume extraction, wash your hands, and keep food out of
  the workshop.
- A solder mask and a silkscreen layer are not insulation for mains
  voltage. A board that connects to the mains must meet the creepage
  and clearance requirements of IPC-2221, and the assembly must use a
  rated fuse, a switch, and an insulated enclosure.
- Test boards from a current-limited supply with the limit set low for
  the first power-up, and never probe a board that is energised from
  the mains with a grounded instrument.
- Reflow ovens and hot plates reach 250 °C; they burn, they fume, and
  they ignite solvents, so keep the area clear and ventilated.
- The board is sharp: the cut edges of the laminate and the exposed
  copper of a broken board cut fingers, so deburr the edges and wash
  off the flux residue.
- Do not rely on the fabricator's assembly for the safety-critical
  parts; check the polarity of the mains-side components and the
  ratings of the fuses yourself.

## Overview

Every piece of electronics needs a source of power that holds inside its
limits while the load changes and the mains does not. Two approaches cover
almost everything: a linear regulator, which is simple and quiet but
throws away the difference between the input and the output voltage as
heat, and a switching converter, which moves power at high frequency and
wastes far less but makes noise on the output and on the mains lead. The
key principle is to size the supply from the heat and the noise the load
can tolerate, not from the rating printed on the case.

## Prerequisites

- DC Circuit Analysis
- AC Circuit Analysis and Impedance
- Reading a semiconductor datasheet
- Soldering and multimeter use

## Materials & Tools

- Step-down transformer, 230 V to 12 V, 25 VA
- Bridge rectifier rated 4 A, or four 1 A, 50 V diodes
- Electrolytic capacitors, 1000 uF at 25 V, 10 uF, and 100 nF
- Linear regulators: 7805, 7812, and one adjustable LM317
- Switching controller with inductor, Schottky diode, and ceramic input
  and output capacitors
- Oscilloscope with a 10X probe, a multimeter, and a resistive load bank
- Heat sink, thermal compound, and a clip-on or infrared thermometer
- Fuse, switch, thermal cut-out, and an earthed chassis

## Procedure

### Size the supply

1. List every load with the voltage it needs, the current it draws there,
   and the tolerance it can live with.
2. Add the currents and multiply by 1.25 to set the supply rating, then
   write down the noise limit, for example under 10 mV of ripple.
3. Compute the heat of a linear stage as (V_in - V_out) x I; 12 V to 5 V
   at 1 A dissipates 7 W and sets the size of the heat sink.

### Build a linear supply

1. Reduce the mains to 12 V AC with the transformer, sized at 1.25 times
   the DC power the load needs.
2. Rectify with the bridge and smooth with the reservoir capacitor; the
   ripple frequency is twice the mains frequency, so 100 Hz at 50 Hz mains.
3. Regulate with the 7805, leaving at least 2 V of headroom above 5 V, and
   place the 100 nF bypass within 10 mm of the regulator pins.

### Build a switching supply

1. Pick the topology: buck to step down, boost to step up, and buck-boost
   when the input may sit on either side of the output.
2. Choose the switching frequency, commonly 50 to 500 kHz, and size the
   inductor so the ripple stays inside the load's tolerance.
3. Keep the input capacitor, the switch, the diode, and the inductor in
   one small loop, because that loop area sets the radiated noise.

### Protect and verify

1. Fit a fuse at about twice the working current, a switch, and a thermal
   cut-out in series with the transformer primary.
2. Check the output with the scope using a spring ground, and confirm the
   ripple is under the limit set in the first stage.
3. Load the output from 10 to 100 percent and record the voltage change
   and the efficiency, then compare both with the datasheet limits.

## Safety Notes

- Mains voltage can kill and can start fires. Work on a mains supply only
  with appropriate training, supervision, and equipment, and keep it
  isolated from the bench while the chassis is open.
- Treat every point of a rectifier output and every heat sink as live; the
  reservoir capacitor can hold a lethal charge for minutes after switch-off.
- Provide at least 2 mm of creepage and clearance across basic insulation
  at mains potential, and 3 mm where reinforced insulation is required.
- Earth the exposed metal of the chassis and never defeat the protective
  earth to make a test pass.
- A reversed electrolytic or a shorted output capacitor can vent and
  burn; check the polarity marks and the voltage ratings before soldering.
- Keep the linear regulator's dissipation below its rating with a heat
  sink and a thermal cut-out, because it has no internal shutdown.
- Never clip an earth-referenced scope ground to a live high-voltage
  switching node; the ground lead is shorted to earth.

and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole

## Overview

Firmware is the program that owns a machine the moment it is powered, and
a real-time operating system is the small layer that decides what runs
when. The key principle is that a deadline is a requirement, not a wish: a
task that must answer in 10 ms has to be scheduled and budgeted, and the
design is finished only when the worst case has been measured on the
target rather than estimated on a desk.

## Prerequisites

- Embedded C and the C standard library
- Reading a microcontroller datasheet and its reference manual
- Binary and hexadecimal numbers, and bit masking
- Basic electronics: logic levels, pull-ups, and open-drain buses

## Materials & Tools

- A supported microcontroller board and a USB debug probe
- The Arm GCC toolchain and a make-based build, or an equivalent
- The FreeRTOS kernel source and the vendor port for the device
- A logic analyser for timing checks and an oscilloscope for analogue
- A multimeter, a solderable prototype board, and jumper wire

## Procedure

### Choose the architecture

1. List every job the firmware must do and the deadline attached to it.
2. Separate the work into tasks by deadline, not by whichever grouping is
   easiest to write.
3. Give the shortest deadline the highest priority, and move slow work out
   of the interrupt context into a task or a deferred handler.

### Write the tasks

1. Give each task its own stack, sized from measured high-water marks
   rather than from a guess, and check those marks at run time.
2. Keep every critical section short and never call a blocking function
   from inside one.
3. Protect shared data with a mutex or a semaphore, and hold it for the
   shortest possible time.
4. Pass data between tasks through a queue where you can, and set the tick
   rate to something the design can afford.

### Meet the deadlines

1. Use a periodic timer interrupt for sampling at a fixed rate and push
   the result into a queue instead of processing it in the handler.
2. Measure the worst-case execution time of every task with a cycle
   counter or with a GPIO toggle read by a logic analyser.
3. Record the jitter of each periodic task over a long run, since a task
   that meets its average but misses its worst case is not finished, and
   enable the watchdog fed from the task that knows the system is alive
   rather than from the interrupt that starts the work.

### Ship and observe

1. Build with optimisation and with debug symbols, keep the map file, and
   assert on the queue depths and the stack high-water marks so the
   numbers are logged over a serial link.
2. Save one binary image per board revision, put the version in a header
   the firmware can read back, and test the power-on path and the
   brown-out path so both land in a known state without a manual reset.

## Safety Notes

- Firmware drives relays, valves, heaters, and motors, so every state the
  machine can enter after a reset must be made safe by hardware, not by
  the code.
- A watchdog fed from an interrupt instead of from the work will not
  catch a hung task.
- A watchdog reset can leave actuators in an unknown state, so define the
  safe state for the reset path explicitly.
- Never trust an unvalidated buffer from a radio or a sensor; bound every
  length and reject malformed frames.
- Removing a debug assertion to ship a release also removes the check it
  was making, so keep the checks and log the failure instead.
- The debug probe and the target share a supply rail, and a mis-wired
  probe can destroy the microcontroller.

*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources

## Overview

Soldering is a controlled chemical join: the solder melts, wets the
copper, and forms a bond that is stronger than either metal alone. The
key principle is that a good joint is made by heat the work can
absorb, so the iron touches the pad and the lead and not the solder,
and the solder is carried in by the heat rather than dropped onto it.
A cold, dull, balled joint is a joint that will fail later and out of
sight, and it costs more than making it properly the first time.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- A temperature-controlled soldering iron of 25 to 60 W, with a nichrome
  or ceramic tip, and a stand with a sponge
- Solder wire of 0.5 to 0.8 mm diameter: 63/37 tin-lead for the classic
  183 °C eutectic, or SAC305 lead-free at 217 °C
- Flux: a rosin pen for general work or a no-clean gel, and separate
  flux for desoldering
- A desoldering pump, desoldering braid, and brass wool for the tip
- Side cutters, needle-nose pliers, a printed circuit board holder, and
  a loupe
- 90% isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free swab for cleaning
- A wrist strap and a grounded mat, and a fume extraction fan
- Heat-shrink tubing, and a multimeter for the continuity checks

## Procedure

### Prepare the iron and the work

1. Set the temperature for the alloy in use: about 320 to 350 °C for a
   leaded joint, and 370 to 400 °C for lead-free work on the larger
   pads, and let the tip warm fully.
2. Wipe the tip with a damp sponge and tin it with a little solder so
   that the heat goes into the work instead of into the tip.
3. Clean the pad and the lead with isopropyl alcohol, and fit the
   component so the lead sits fully in the hole with no strain on the
   joint.

### Make the joint

1. Heat the pad and the lead together for two or three seconds and
   keep the iron still; the solder should flow onto the pad and up the
   lead, not form a ball on the iron tip.
2. Feed the solder into the heated joint, not onto the iron, and stop
   feeding as soon as the fillet forms and the solder runs down the
   lead.
3. Take the iron away along the direction of the lead so that the
   solder does not stick to the tip, hold the component still for two
   or three seconds while the joint cools, and clean and re-tin the
   tip before moving to the next joint.

### Inspect the joint

1. Check the fillet under magnification: the surface must be smooth and
   concave, with a contact angle of 90 degrees or less, and there must
   be no ball, no crack, and no void in the fillet.
2. Check the wetting of the lead: for a through-hole joint on a 0.6 mm
   lead, at least 75% of the lead length should be wetted and the hole
   filled, which is the acceptance level for a dedicated-service
   product.
3. Flex the board gently and check for a cracked joint, then measure
   the continuity from the pad to the component lead on every joint
   that matters.

### Rework and desolder

1. For a through-hole part, apply flux to the joint, heat the pad and
   the lead together, and pull the lead with the iron against the pad
   until it releases; add fresh solder to the joint to keep it wet.
2. For a pad that will not release, wick the joint with desoldering
   braid and a hot iron, or use a desoldering pump, then clean the pad
   with isopropyl alcohol.
3. Pad the board flat, tinned copper side up, on a heat-resistant
   surface, keep the iron moving so that the laminate does not scorch,
   and re-tin any pad that has been drawn down before refitting the
   part.

## Safety Notes

- The iron tip sits at 250 to 400 °C and molten solder sticks to skin
  and burns through it. Use a stand, rest the iron on a heat-resistant
  surface, and never leave it in the holder unattended.
- Flux smoke and solder vapour are irritants and can cause asthma with
  repeated exposure. Work with local fume extraction or in the open
  air, and never solder in a sealed room.
- Lead and lead-containing solder are cumulative poisons. Wash your
  hands after soldering, do not eat or drink in the work area, and
  keep the solder out of reach of children.
- Isopropyl alcohol and the tip cleaners are flammable; keep them away
  from the hot iron and away from any open flame.
- The desoldering pump and the hot braid spit molten solder; point
  them away from your face and wear eye protection.
- Work on mains-connected boards only with the supply unplugged and
  discharged, and never touch a live board with a grounded tool such
  as an oscilloscope earth clip.
- Solder spatter and flux splatter burn; wear eye protection and keep
  the bench clear.

## Overview

Testing is how a claim about a system becomes evidence that somebody else
can check. The key principle is that a test is worth exactly what its
independent oracle is worth: an assertion that repeats the code under test
proves nothing. Good suites fail when the code is wrong, keep failing
until it is fixed, and are cheap enough to run on every change.

## Prerequisites

- The requirements the system must meet, written down
- A defect log and a way to reproduce each fault
- Basic programming and the ability to read a test report

## Materials & Tools

- A test runner for the language in use, and a version control system
- An environment that can be rebuilt from nothing, such as a container
  image or a provisioning script
- Interface and load generators for the hardware case
- A logic analyser, a multimeter, and a thermal camera for power work
- A coverage tool, and test data held in version control

## Procedure

### Write the test

1. Write the acceptance criterion as a single checkable statement before
   you write any code.
2. Choose the level: unit for a calculation, integration for a boundary,
   system for a whole workflow, and acceptance for the user's goal.
3. Make the test deterministic by fixing time, randomness, and ordering,
   and by injecting those instead of mocking them.
4. Give every test one clear failure message that names the expected value
   and the observed value, then confirm the test can fail by changing the
   code and watching it turn red.

### Build the suite

1. Put many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests above
   them, and a small number of slow end-to-end tests on top.
2. Give each test its own fixtures so the order never matters, then
   randomise the order to prove that it does not.
3. Keep the hardware-in-the-loop tests behind a tag so a bench run does
   not slow the daily loop.
4. Store the test data and the expected results in version control next
   to the code that reads them.

### Measure and act

1. Measure line, branch, and requirement coverage, and treat a coverage
   number as a pointer to untested code rather than as a target.
2. Track the number of defects each test finds and the time each test
   takes, and fix the slow ones before they slow everyone down.
3. Run the suite on every change and treat a red build as the only signal
   that matters.
4. Keep a defect log with the reproduction steps, the version, and the
   date, and never close a defect without a test that would have caught
   it.

## Safety Notes

- Tests are not a licence to run hardware beyond its ratings; the test
  bench has the same current, voltage, and temperature limits as the
  product.
- A test that energises an actuator must have a defined safe state and a
  physical way to stop it.
- Fault-injection tests on mains or battery circuits can start fires, so
  use a current-limited source and a supervised test area.
- Keep test data free of real credentials, personal data, and live keys;
  use synthetic records.
- A test skipped today is a defect with a delayed report, so track skips
  the same way as failures.
- Do not let the mock in a test become a second, untested implementation
  of the thing you are checking.

## Overview

Bridges cross water or ravines. Span length dictates the type: simple beam for
short spans, trusses for medium, and suspension for long spans.

## Prerequisites

- Timber Framing
- Rope & Cordage

## Materials & Tools

- Heavy timbers or steel
- Stone abutments
- Rope or cable
- Fasteners and pegs

## Procedure

### Surveying the Crossing

1. Measure span, bank height, and flood level.
2. Choose an abutment site on firm ground above flood stage.

### Beam Bridge

1. Build abutments of stone or concrete.
2. Lay one or more beams across, sized by span and load.
3. Deck with planks and add railings.

### Truss or Suspension

1. Assemble a truss on the bank and roll it into place.
2. For suspension, anchor cables to deadmen and hang the deck.
3. Load-test gradually before allowing traffic.

## Safety Notes

- Red hazard: structural failure is often fatal; over-build and load-test.
- Never work over moving water without fall protection and a spotter.

source of information.*

## Overview

A composting toilet stores human waste with enough carbon cover and time for
pathogens to die off while it decomposes. Twin vaults let one batch cure while
the other is in use. The design must control moisture, ventilation, and
leachate; a smelly or wet toilet is a sign that the process is failing.

## Prerequisites

- Latrine siting and sanitation knowledge
- Basic masonry or carpentry skills
- A source of dry carbon cover

## Materials & Tools

- Concrete, brick, or rot-resistant timber for twin vaults
- Impermeable vault floor and leachate collection
- Vent pipe with fly screen and rain cap
- Toilet pedestal and urine-diverting seat if used
- Sawdust, ash, dry leaves, or straw cover
- Lid, steps, and handwashing station
- Gloves, boots, and cleaning tools
- Thermometer and moisture test

## Procedure

### 1. Site and design

1. Keep the toilet at least 30 m from wells and surface water, and downslope of
   drinking-water sources.
2. Choose a site above the water table and away from flood paths.
3. Size each vault for at least one year of use by the household.
4. Provide access for emptying and a separate handwashing point.

### 2. Build the vaults

1. Cast or lay a level, impermeable floor with a slight slope to a leachate
   sump.
2. Build two sealed vaults with removable covers and a shared pedestal that can
   be switched when one fills.
3. Run a vent pipe from each vault to above the roof; screen the top and keep it
   open.
4. Fit a fly-proof seat and a tight lid; keep rainwater out.

### 3. Operate the toilet

1. Add a cup of dry cover after every use; keep a bucket beside the seat.
2. Divert urine separately if the design allows; do not flood the vault.
3. Keep the vault moist like a wrung-out sponge, not wet.
4. Empty the full vault only after it has cured for 12-24 months.

### 4. Cure and use the product

1. Move cured material to a covered curing bin; protect it from rain and
   animals.
2. Test temperature and moisture; turn the pile if it is too wet.
3. Use finished compost on perennial crops or ornamental plants, not on
   ready-to-eat vegetables.
4. Clean tools and hands, and change clothes after handling.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Human waste carries pathogens. Wear gloves and boots, keep
  the site fly-proof, and wash hands after every contact.
- Leachate can contaminate groundwater; collect and treat it separately.
- Do not use fresh or partially cured material on food crops.
- Vaults can accumulate methane and ammonia; ventilate before opening and never
  enter a vault.

## Overview

Safe excreta disposal prevents cholera, typhoid, and intestinal worms. A
fly-proof latrine and a handwashing point are the highest-impact sanitation
interventions in any settlement.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Shovel
- Slab or timber cover
- Vent pipe and screen
- Water and soap or ash

## Procedure

### Pit Latrine

1. Dig a pit at least 1 m deep, away from wells (>=30 m) and downhill.
2. Fit a squat slab with a tight drop hole.
3. Build a shelter for privacy and a roof to keep rain out.

### Ventilated Improved Pit

1. Run a vent pipe from the pit to above the roof.
2. Screen the pipe top to trap flies.

### Handwashing Station

1. Set a tippy-tap or bucket with a spout near the exit.
2. Provide soap or wood ash before eating and after defecation.

## Safety Notes

- Never site pits uphill or within 30 m of a water source.
- Wash hands with soap; ash is an acceptable substitute.

## Overview

Masonry builds durable walls, foundations, and ovens from stone or brick bedded
in lime or cement mortar. Correct bond and footing prevent collapse.

## Prerequisites

- Lime & Cement
- Brick Making

## Materials & Tools

- Stone or fired brick
- Lime or cement mortar
- Level, trowel, and string line

## Procedure

### Footing

1. Dig a trench below frost depth and fill with rubble set in mortar.
2. Level the first course carefully; every error propagates upward.

### Laying Units

1. Spread a mortar bed and place each unit, tapping it level.
2. Stagger joints (running bond) and keep the wall plumb with a string line.
3. Rake joints when mortar is thumb-dry, then point them.

### Curing

1. Keep masonry damp for several days to prevent cracking.
2. Cover in freezing weather until mortar hardens.

## Safety Notes

- Lime and cement are caustic; wear gloves and eye protection.
- Never build tall unsupported walls; brace until cured.

## Overview

All-weather roads move goods and people and connect settlements. The key is a
crowned surface with side ditches so water leaves the roadbed quickly.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Gravel or crushed stone
- Hand tools and barrows
- Logs or culverts

## Procedure

### Alignment & Clearing

1. Lay out a route along ridges or valley sides, crossing streams at right angles.
2. Clear vegetation and topsoil from a 4-6 m corridor.

### Construction

1. Cut side ditches and crown the roadbed to shed water.
2. Spread and compact gravel in layers, largest stones at the base.
3. Install culverts at every drainage crossing.

## Safety Notes

- Brace trench sides during excavation.
- Keep ditches clear; a blocked ditch destroys a road in one storm.

## Overview

A root cellar uses earth's stable temperature and high humidity to keep root
crops, apples, cabbages, and preserves through winter. A 2 m x 3 m cellar holds
roughly 1,500-2,500 kg. The design must balance insulation, ventilation, and
moisture: too warm and crops sprout or rot, too dry and they shrivel, too wet
and mould wins.

## Prerequisites

- Simple housing and earthwork experience
- A well-drained site

## Materials & Tools

- Stone or concrete block
- Timber or concrete roof
- Insulation
- Vent pipes with insect screen
- Gravel floor
- Shelving and slatted crates
- Thermometer and hygrometer
- Rodent mesh

## Procedure

### 1. Site and design

1. Choose a slope or high spot with good drainage; never a hollow that floods.
2. Keep the cellar away from septic fields, wells, and tree roots.
3. Plan two vents: a low inlet and a high outlet for natural convection.
4. Size for the harvest: about 0.5-0.7 tonnes per cubic metre of usable space.

### 2. Excavate and line

1. Mark the footprint and excavate with stable, sloped sides.
2. Shore the walls before digging deeper than 1 m.
3. Build block or stone walls with a footing; leave weep holes and a gravel
   drain.
4. Seal the outside against surface water and insulate the roof and upper
   walls.

### 3. Roof, door, and vents

1. Build a strong roof that can carry soil and snow load.
2. Fit an insulated, tight-fitting door; avoid a direct path for warm air.
3. Install screened vents with adjustable dampers.
4. Cover the roof with earth and vegetation, leaving the vents clear.

### 4. Load and manage

1. Cure root crops for a few days before storage; remove damaged produce.
2. Store in slatted crates off the floor, separated by crop and date.
3. Keep the temperature near 0-4 C and humidity at 85-95%.
4. Vent at night when outside air is colder; close vents in warm weather.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Excavations collapse. Shore walls and never let anyone work
  alone below ground.
- Carbon dioxide can accumulate in a sealed cellar. Open the door and ventilate
  before entering; use a lantern test or gas monitor.
- Mouldy produce releases spores; remove spoilage and wear a mask.
- Keep rodents out with mesh and concrete; they contaminate food and gnaw
  wiring.

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Most earthquake injuries come from falling objects, failed chimneys, and houses
sliding off their foundations, not from the ground opening up. Bracing a house
means tying it to its foundation, strengthening weak walls, and securing heavy
contents. The work must suit the building type; retrofits that look strong but
create a stiff, brittle storey can make damage worse.

## Prerequisites

- Structural assessment of the building
- Carpentry, masonry, and anchoring skills
- A plan approved by a local engineer where required

## Materials & Tools

- Foundation anchor bolts, plates, and epoxy
- Metal straps, brackets, and hold-downs
- Structural screws and nails
- Plywood or oriented strand board for shear walls
- Water heater straps and flexible gas connectors
- Cabinet latches and shelf restraints
- Drill, impact driver, wrench, and level

## Procedure

### 1. Assess and plan

1. Identify the foundation type, wall construction, roof, and any soft storey.
2. Check for existing rot, cracks, and prior unpermitted alterations.
3. Mark the load path from roof to foundation; every brace must connect.
4. Have an engineer review plans for unreinforced masonry or hillside sites.

### 2. Tie the house down

1. Install foundation anchors through the sill plate at the spacing specified
   by the engineer.
2. Add hold-downs at corners and wall ends where uplift and racking are highest.
3. Strap the roof to the walls and the walls to the floor framing.
4. Reinforce cripple walls with plywood sheathing and blocking.

### 3. Brace chimneys and heavy contents

1. Brace or replace unreinforced masonry chimneys; secure the flue.
2. Strap the water heater to wall studs with two metal straps and keep the gas
   connector flexible.
3. Anchor bookcases, cabinets, and tall furniture to studs.
4. Store heavy items low and latch cabinet doors.

### 4. Check and maintain

1. Inspect anchors and straps after any earthquake or nearby construction.
2. Look for new cracks, loose bolts, and water damage.
3. Re-tighten fasteners to the specified torque; do not overtighten wood.
4. Keep a written retrofit plan and photographs for future repairs.

## Safety Notes

- **Yellow hazard:** Retrofitting involves power tools, dust, and work at height.
  Wear eye and hearing protection and use stable ladders.
- Do not cut structural members without engineering advice.
- Gas leaks and damaged chimneys are fire and explosion hazards after a quake.
- Unreinforced masonry can collapse suddenly; keep people out of the work zone.

title: Simple Housing
materialsRequired: Posts and beams (rot-resistant timber or treated poles)
Wattle, cordwood, adobe, or log infill
Roof thatch, shingles, or earth
Stone or rubble for footings
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Permanent shelter protects against weather, pests, and temperature swings. A
dry, ventilated, raised-floor structure with a sound roof and a hearth is enough
for most climates.

## Prerequisites

- Emergency Shelter
- Rope & Cordage

## Materials & Tools

- Posts and beams (rot-resistant timber or treated poles)
- Wattle, cordwood, adobe, or log infill
- Roof thatch, shingles, or earth
- Stone or rubble for footings

## Procedure

### Site & Footings

1. Choose level, well-drained ground above flood lines.
2. Clear vegetation and mark a rectangle with corner stakes and string.
3. Set corner posts on dry-stacked stone footings to keep wood off the soil.

### Frame & Walls

1. Set vertical posts at 1.5-2 m spacing and brace them plumb.
2. Add a top plate and gable rafters.
3. Infill walls with wattle-and-daub, cordwood, or stacked logs.

### Roof & Floor

1. Lay purlins across the rafters and cover with thatch, shingles, or sod.
2. Overlap roofing layers so water always runs downhill.
3. Raise the floor 20-30 cm on joists and pack the crawl space with dry stone.

## Safety Notes

- Never burn unseasoned or resinous wood in a sealed room without ventilation.
- Treat all framing against insects and rot where possible.

## Overview

Surveying sets out boundaries, grades, and alignments accurately. Simple
leveling and angle measurement suffice for most community works.

## Prerequisites

- None

## Materials & Tools

- Level (water or dumpy)
- Measuring chain or tape
- Range poles and pegs

## Procedure

### Leveling

1. Use a water level (clear hose) or dumpy level to transfer elevations.
2. Record backsight, foresight, and rise/fall for each station.

### Setting Out

1. Establish a baseline and square it with the 3-4-5 method.
2. Offset to locate corners and alignments.
3. Mark stations with stakes and reference ties.

## Safety Notes

title: Timber Framing
materialsRequired: Seasoned structural timber
Hardwood pegs
Chisels, augers, and a bow saw
Mallet and framing square
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Timber framing joins heavy members with interlocking mortise-and-tenon joints
and pegs. A well-cut frame carries roof and floor loads without nails or steel.

## Prerequisites

- Simple Tools

## Materials & Tools

- Seasoned structural timber
- Hardwood pegs
- Chisels, augers, and a bow saw
- Mallet and framing square

## Procedure

### Layout

1. Square a frame on the ground using the 3-4-5 method.
2. Mark joints with a numbering system before cutting.

### Cutting Joints

1. Bore and chop mortises one-third the member's thickness.
2. Cut tenons to a snug fit; test each joint dry before assembly.

### Raising

1. Assemble bents flat, then raise them with props and pegs.
2. Join bents with girts and purlins, checking plumb and level.
3. Pin every joint with a draw-bored hardwood peg.

## Safety Notes

- Work with a spotter when raising bents; keep clear of falling members.
- Keep edged tools sheathed when not cutting.

title: Water Wells
materialsRequired: Lining (stone, brick, or concrete rings)
Pump or bucket hoist

body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

A well taps groundwater for a reliable supply. The method depends on depth: dug
wells for shallow aquifers, driven and bored wells for sand, and drilled wells
for deep rock.

## Prerequisites

- Finding Water

## Materials & Tools

- Lining (stone, brick, or concrete rings)
- Pump or bucket hoist
- Rope and bucket

## Procedure

### Locating the Aquifer

1. Sight wells in low ground near streams, springs, or green vegetation.
2. Confirm with dowsing-free methods: test pits and local knowledge.

### Dug Well

1. Excavate a shaft 1 m wide, lining as you descend to prevent collapse.
2. Stop at the water table and line the intake with gravel.
3. Build a curb 50 cm above grade and cap to keep surface water out.

### Finishing

1. Backfill around the lining with clay to shed surface water.
2. Disinfect the well with chlorine and test before drinking.

## Safety Notes

- Dug wells can collapse or accumulate toxic gas; always have a spotter.
- Treat all well water as contaminated until disinfected.

title: Battery Basics
materialsRequired: Lead plates (grid + active material)
Sulfuric acid (30% H₂SO₄)
Case (plastic or hard rubber)
Separators (porous rubber, glass mat)
Terminals
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Batteries store electrical energy chemically. Lead-acid is the most
rebuildable chemistry; lithium-ion is denser but harder to make from scratch.

## Prerequisites

- [Metal Smelting](../materials/metal-smelting.md)
- [Chemistry](../materials/chemistry.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Lead plates (grid + active material)
- Sulfuric acid (30% H₂SO₄)
- Case (plastic or hard rubber)
- Separators (porous rubber, glass mat)
- Terminals

## Procedure

### Lead-Acid Cell (2 V per cell)

1. Cast lead grids; paste with lead oxide (positive) and sponge lead (negative).
2. Stack alternating plates with separators.
3. Weld straps to terminals.
4. Fill with 30% sulfuric acid.
5. **Formation charge:** slow charge for 24 hours to convert pastes.

### 6 Cells = 12 V Battery

- 6 cells in series → 12 V nominal.
- Capacity: Ah = plate area × number of plates.

### Charging

1. **Bulk:** constant current to 14.4 V.
2. **Absorption:** constant voltage 14.4 V until current drops to 3% of capacity.
3. **Float:** 13.6 V to maintain.

### Maintenance

- Top up with distilled water monthly.
- Equalize every 1–3 months (15.5 V for 2 hours).
- Never discharge below 50% (12.1 V).
- Keep terminals clean; grease them.

### Other Chemistries

- **NiFe (Edison):** 1.2 V/cell; nearly indestructible; low efficiency.
- **NiCd:** 1.2 V/cell; toxic cadmium.
- **LiFePO₄:** 3.2 V/cell; safe; requires BMS.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Sulfuric acid burns. Lead is neurotoxic.
  Wear gloves, goggles, apron. Work outdoors.
- **Explosive hydrogen** during charging — ventilate.
- Never short terminals; never reverse polarity.
- Dispose of lead and acid properly.

title: Biogas Digester
materialsRequired: Digester (fixed-dome, floating-drum, or tubular)
Feedstock: manure, food scraps
Water
Gas storage (bag or drum)
Stove or generator
body:
*Reference material only. Verify this information against primary sources
and qualified professionals before acting on it. This entry is not a sole
source of information.*

## Overview

Anaerobic digestion of manure, food waste, and crop residue produces biogas
(60% CH₄, 40% CO₂) plus a nutrient-rich effluent for fertilizer.

## Prerequisites

- [Raising Livestock](../agriculture/raising-livestock.md)
- [Fire & Combustion](fire-combustion.md)

## Materials & Tools

- Digester (fixed-dome, floating-drum, or tubular)
- Feedstock: manure, food scraps
- Water
- Gas storage (bag or drum)
- Stove or generator

## Procedure

### Fixed-Dome (Deenbandhu)

1. Dig a pit 2–3 m diameter, 2 m deep.
2. Build brick or concrete dome over the top with a gas outlet.
3. Inlet pipe at bottom for slurry.
4. Outlet pipe for effluent at ⅔ height.
5. Volume: 1 m³ per cow per day.

### Floating-Drum

1. Dig a cylindrical pit.
2. Place a steel drum inverted over the top — it rises with gas pressure.
3. Gas outlet from drum top.

### Tubular (Flexible)

1. Lay a long plastic or rubber bag in a trench.
2. Fill ⅔ with slurry.
3. Gas collects at the top; use a weighted bag for pressure.

### Feeding

- Cow manure: 1:1 with water
- Pig manure: 1:2 with water
- Food waste: pre-compost, then feed
- C:N ratio: 20–30:1
- pH: 6.8–7.4
- Temperature: 30–40°C (mesophilic)

### Retention Time

- 15–30 days at 35°C.
- 40–60 days at 20°C.

### Using Biogas

- Burn directly in a stove (adjust air for methane).
- 1 m³ biogas ≈ 0.6 L petrol ≈ 6 kWh.
- 1 cow yields ~0.4 m³/day.

## Safety Notes

- **Red hazard:** Biogas is explosive (5–15% in air) and can asphyxiate.
  Never enter a digester pit — H₂S and CO₂ displace oxygen.
- Keep flames away from gas leaks.
- Ventilate any enclosed gas equipment.
- Effluent is caustic; wear gloves.
